name: Presocratics

tagline.text: The first Greek thinkers to explain nature by reasoned inquiry instead of myth.

description: The first Greek thinkers to explain the natural world and its principles by reasoned inquiry rather than myth.
debatable: A modern label: SEP says the term was coined in the 18th century and made current by Diels, and that the last 'Presocratics' were contemporaries of Socrates. The Sophists are folded in here (SEP covers them in the same entry, §9).

questions.text: Underneath all the change I see, what is everything really made of?
Can I explain a rainbow or a storm without saying the gods did it?

questions.text: How far can my senses, and my own reasoning, get me to the truth?

themes.title: Nature without myth
themes.text: These thinkers saw the world as a kosmos: an ordered, natural arrangement that makes sense on its own terms. Where the old poets had gods stepping in, they looked for causes inside nature itself. Xenophanes, for example, said the rainbow is simply coloured cloud.

themes.title: What things are made of
themes.text: Many of them looked for one basic stuff or principle (the Greeks called it the archē) behind everything. Thales is reported to have said water; Heraclitus pointed to fire; the atomists said solid, uncuttable bodies separated by empty space (the void).

themes.title: Everything flows
themes.text: Heraclitus taught that the world is constant change held together by a hidden order, which he called the logos (the rational account of how things work). Opposites like up and down, or waking and sleeping, turn out to be bound together.

sources.section: 3. Xenophanes of Colophon and Heraclitus of Ephesus

themes.title: Reality versus appearance
themes.text: Parmenides argued that real knowledge is about what is and cannot fail to be, and that the senses give us only belief. Democritus also split appearance from reality: tastes and colours are a matter of convention, while what really exists is atoms and void.

themes.title: Caring for the soul
themes.text: Natural inquiry sat alongside questions about how to live. Pythagoras seems to have taught that the soul is reborn after death and founded a strict way of life; Heraclitus thought a dry, fiery soul was wisest; Democritus was linked with the ideal of good cheer.

reacted_against.text: The god-filled stories of poets like Hesiod, where the world comes from divine family feuds and the gods meddle in the weather and in human life.

thinkers.name: Thales of Miletus
thinkers.summary: Thales of Miletus seems to have lived around the start of the 6th century BCE. Aristotle names him as the first person to look for the basic causes and principles of nature. He apparently wrote no book, so we know him mostly through later reports, and the famous story that he predicted an eclipse is almost certainly not true.

key_ideas.text: He held that water is the first principle (archē), the stuff from which everything comes.

sources.section: 3. Thales says Water is the Primary Principle

key_ideas.text: He explained nature by nature itself, with no gods stepping in from outside.
He is reported to have said the magnetic lodestone has a soul because it moves iron, and that all things are full of gods.

sources.section: 7. All Things are Full of God

study_prompt.text: Teach me Thales of Miletus as a short Socratic module. Start with a Greek from Miletus around the start of the 6th century BCE whom Aristotle called the first natural philosopher, then his three key ideas: water as the first principle of all things; explaining nature without outside divine intervention; the lodestone's soul and the report that all things are full of gods. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 3. Thales says Water is the Primary Principle

thinkers.name: Pythagoras of Samos
thinkers.dates: fl. last quarter of the 6th c. BCE
thinkers.summary: Pythagoras grew up on the island of Samos and moved to Croton in southern Italy, where he gathered a community of followers. He wrote nothing, and later writers turned him into a near-divine figure, so his real views are hard to recover. In his own time he was famous for teachings about the soul and a strict way of life, not for mathematics.

key_ideas.text: The soul is immortal and is reborn again and again, possibly even in animals.
He founded a disciplined way of life with dietary rules, religious ritual and self-control.
The cosmos may be ordered by number and musical ratios, though how much of this was his own is doubtful.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Pythagoras of Samos as a short Socratic module. Start with a teacher from Samos who founded a community in Croton in the late 6th century BCE, then his three key ideas: the soul's rebirth into new bodies; a disciplined Pythagorean way of life; a cosmos ordered by number, and how much of that is really his. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Heraclitus of Ephesus
thinkers.summary: Heraclitus of Ephesus was active around 500 BCE and is said to have written a single book, likely made up mostly of short, riddling sayings. He is best known for the ideas that things are always changing, that opposites belong together, and that fire is the world's basic stuff. He hints that he was self-taught, and he is hard to fit into any school.

key_ideas.text: On one leading reading, some things stay the same only by changing, like a river that remains a river because new water keeps flowing.
Opposites are bound together: sea water is healthy for fish but harmful for people.

sources.section: 3. Xenophanes of Colophon and Heraclitus of Ephesus

key_ideas.text: One rational order, the logos, steers everything, and fire is its sign.

sources.section: 3. Xenophanes of Colophon and Heraclitus of Ephesus

study_prompt.text: Teach me Heraclitus of Ephesus as a short Socratic module. Start with a philosopher of Ephesus active around 500 BCE who wrote in riddles, then his three key ideas: on one leading reading, staying the same by changing, as a river does; the unity of opposites; the logos that steers everything, with fire as its sign. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Parmenides of Elea
thinkers.summary: Parmenides was born around 510 BCE in Elea, a Greek colony in southern Italy. He wrote a poem in which a goddess teaches a young man how to tell truth from mere belief. It has earned him a reputation as one of the deepest and hardest of the early Greek thinkers, and he is often seen as forcing later thinkers to answer his arguments.

key_ideas.text: There are only two routes of inquiry, that something is or that it is not, and you cannot know what is not.
Whatever truly is cannot come into being or pass away; it is whole, unshaken and complete.
Judge by reasoning, not by habit, eyes and ears; perception gives only belief, not knowledge.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Parmenides of Elea as a short Socratic module. Start with a poet-philosopher from Elea in southern Italy, born around 510 BCE, then his three key ideas: the two routes, what is and what is not; what truly is cannot be born or perish, and is whole, unshaken and complete; reason over the senses, knowledge over belief. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Democritus
thinkers.summary: Democritus was born about 460 BCE in Abdera in northern Greece. He built on a system begun by his teacher Leucippus: atomism, the theory that everything is built from tiny indivisible bodies moving in empty space. His works survive only in second-hand reports, and in antiquity he was known as the 'laughing philosopher' for prizing cheerfulness.

key_ideas.text: Only atoms and void are real; things differ by the shape, position and arrangement of their atoms.
Tastes, colours and heat exist by convention; the senses give a second-rate knowledge that reason must interpret.
The good is an inner state of cheerfulness, helped by moderating desire.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Democritus as a short Socratic module. Start with a thinker from Abdera born about 460 BCE who built on the atomism begun by his teacher Leucippus, then his three key ideas: atoms and void as all that is real; sweet and bitter by convention, and two kinds of knowing; cheerfulness as the goal of life. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

tagline.text: Socrates' questioning and Plato's dialogues on the Forms behind what we see.

sources.section: 2. The Socratic problem: Who was Socrates really?

description: Socrates' questioning method and Plato's dialogues, including the split between the many things we observe and the one Form each shares in, which SEP calls the most fundamental distinction in Plato's philosophy.

questions.text: Is a life I never stop to examine really worth living?
Do I actually know the things I think I know?
Is there a truer reality behind the world I see and touch?

themes.title: Question everything
themes.text: Socrates tested people's beliefs by cross-examining them, a method called the elenchus (asking 'what is it?' and then probing the answer). He claimed no expert knowledge himself; his wisdom was knowing that he did not know.

sources.section: a. The Elenchus: Socrates the Refuter

themes.title: Care for your soul
themes.text: Socrates urged his fellow Athenians to care for their souls more than for money, reputation or their bodies. Plato went further and treated the soul as a different kind of thing from the body, able to exist without it.

sources.section: ii. Priority of the Care of the Soul

themes.title: Virtue is knowledge
themes.text: Socrates argued that the virtues are really one, and that virtue is a kind of knowledge. On this view no one does wrong knowingly; doing wrong is a failure to know what is good.

sources.section: i. Unity of Virtue; All Virtue is Knowledge
ii. No One Errs Knowingly/No One Errs Willingly

themes.title: The Forms
themes.text: Plato held that the world of the senses is flawed, and that behind it stand the Forms: eternal, unchanging patterns like beauty or justice itself. Beautiful things are beautiful because they relate to Beauty itself.

themes.title: Who was the real Socrates?
themes.text: Socrates wrote nothing, so we meet him through others, mainly Plato, Xenophon and the comic playwright Aristophanes, whose portraits differ a lot. Untangling the historical man from these portraits is called the Socratic problem, and it may never be solved.

sources.section: 2. The Socratic problem: Who was Socrates really?

reacted_against.text: The Sophists, paid teachers who claimed to teach success and virtue, and the cosmological inquiries into things in the sky and below the earth that were the main focus of many Presocratic thinkers.

thinkers.name: Socrates
thinkers.summary: Socrates (469–399 BCE) wrote nothing, yet he is considered one of the few philosophers who changed how philosophy itself was conceived. He spent his days in the Athenian marketplace, questioning anyone who would talk about courage, love, reverence, moderation and the state of their soul, and he refused to take money for it. Athens executed him on a charge of irreverence toward the gods.

key_ideas.text: Knowing that you don't know is wiser than believing you know when you don't.
The health of your soul matters more than wealth, reputation or your body.

sources.section: ii. Priority of the Care of the Soul

key_ideas.text: No one does wrong knowingly; wrongdoing comes from not knowing what is good.

Start with the Athenian street philosopher of 469–399 BCE who wrote nothing and was executed for irreverence, then his three key ideas: Socratic ignorance, knowing that you do not know; care of the soul above wealth and reputation; no one does wrong knowingly. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Xenophon
thinkers.summary: Xenophon was a soldier and historian who, like Plato, wrote works starring Socrates, including an Apology and the Memorabilia. He probably spent much less time with Socrates than Plato did, and he left Athens for good in 401. His Socrates is a practical adviser, and scholars still argue over how far that portrait can be trusted.

key_ideas.text: Socrates appears as a practical adviser, even on making money and running an estate.
Self-mastery (enkrateia, control over one's desires) is the foundation of virtue.
You are rich when you need little, not when you have much.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Xenophon as a short Socratic module. Start with a soldier-historian of the early 4th century BCE who wrote his own memoirs of Socrates, then his three key ideas: Socrates as a practical adviser; self-mastery as the foundation of virtue; being rich by needing little. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Plato
thinkers.summary: Plato (429?–347 BCE) was a high-status Athenian and one of the most influential writers in the history of philosophy. He wrote dialogues in nearly all of which Socrates speaks, often as the principal speaker, so it is hard to say where his teacher ends and he begins. Philosophy as a rigorous, systematic study of ethics, politics, reality and knowledge can fairly be called his invention.

key_ideas.text: Behind the many things we see is a more real realm of Forms, perfect and unchanging patterns such as Beauty itself.
The soul is different from the body, and in some dialogues it recollects what it grasped of the Forms before birth.
Philosophy should improve political life: the Republic attacks rule by the many, while the later Laws gives non-philosophers real power as rulers.

sources.section: 10. Does Plato change his mind about politics?

Start with the Athenian writer of dialogues, 429?–347 BCE, whose conception of philosophy as a rigorous, systematic discipline can be called his invention, then his three key ideas: the Forms behind the world we see; the soul as distinct from the body, and recollection; reforming the city, from the Republic to the Laws. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Aristotle and the Peripatetics

tagline.text: Aristotle's wide-ranging study of logic, nature, ethics and politics, at the Lyceum.

description: Aristotle's wide-ranging philosophy, from logic and metaphysics to ethics, politics and the study of plants and animals, taught at his school, the Lyceum.
debatable: Centred on one great thinker, Aristotle; his school, the Lyceum, whose members later came to be called Peripatetics, gives it school status.

questions.text: What does a human life need in order to go well?
When I ask why something is the way it is, what would count as a full answer?

sources.section: 7. The Four Causal Account of Explanatory Adequacy

questions.text: Do living things grow toward goals, even if nobody designed them?

themes.title: Start from wonder
themes.text: Aristotle thought philosophy begins in wonder at puzzling things. He trusted our senses and minds to be mostly reliable, so he started from how the world appears and what others had said about it, then worked through the puzzles.

themes.title: Four kinds of 'why'
themes.text: To explain a thing fully, Aristotle asked four questions: what it is made of, what form or pattern it has, what brought it about, and what it is for. A bronze statue, for example, has bronze, a shape, a sculptor and a purpose.

sources.section: 7. The Four Causal Account of Explanatory Adequacy

themes.title: Purpose in nature
themes.text: Aristotle held that nature works toward ends without any designer: leaves grow to shade fruit, spiders spin webs for a reason. His successor Theophrastus asked whether every natural thing really has a purpose.

themes.title: Flourishing in a community
themes.text: The best life is eudaimonia (happiness or flourishing): using reason, and using it excellently. Humans are political animals who flourish only inside a well-ordered city.

themes.title: The soul as the body's form
themes.text: For Aristotle the soul is not a separate thing living in the body but the form that makes a body alive and organized. Alexander of Aphrodisias later read the human soul as the perishable form of the body.

reacted_against.text: Plato's theory of Forms, which Aristotle thought could not explain change and coming-to-be, and the earlier thinkers who explained life by matter alone.

links.label: Academy student, then Forms critic
links.reason: Aristotle studied in Plato's Academy before founding the Lyceum. Then: Aristotle criticised Plato's theory of Forms (it cannot explain change) and opposed Platonic dualism of soul and body.

links.label: early materialism rejected
links.reason: Aristotle saw the Presocratics as his predecessors but judged them unsuccessful, and rejected their materialist accounts of living things.

links.label: non-rational soul rejected
links.reason: Stoic psychology rejects the Platonic-Aristotelian idea of non-rational parts of the mature soul.

links.label: Aristotle's Metaphysics as starting point
links.reason: Plotinus used passages of Aristotle's Metaphysics as starting points, and his sessions read commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.

links.label: Aristotle rediscovered
links.reason: Thirteenth-century university philosophers were enthused by newly available Aristotle; Aquinas worked to write commentaries on all of Aristotle's principal works.

thinkers.name: Aristotle
thinkers.summary: Aristotle (384–322 BCE) came from Stagira in northern Greece and studied at Plato's Academy until Plato died in 347. He later tutored the young Alexander the Great, then returned to Athens in 335 and founded his own school, the Lyceum, whose members became known as Peripatetics. About thirty-one of his works survive, ranging from logic and ethics to close observation of plants and animals.

key_ideas.text: To explain a thing fully, give its four causes: its matter, its form, what made it, and what it is for.

sources.section: 7. The Four Causal Account of Explanatory Adequacy

key_ideas.text: Nature has goals without a designer; living things develop parts for the sake of something.
Happiness is reason-guided activity done excellently, and humans flourish only within a political community.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Aristotle as a short Socratic module. Start with Plato's student from Stagira, 384–322 BCE, who founded the Lyceum, then his three key ideas: the four causes; purpose in nature without design; happiness as excellent rational activity in a community. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 7. The Four Causal Account of Explanatory Adequacy

thinkers.name: Theophrastus
thinkers.summary: Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BCE) was born on Lesbos, met Aristotle at Plato's Academy, and became his close colleague and his successor at the Lyceum. He is credited with over two hundred treatises, but less than a tenth survives. He worked to support, improve and extend Aristotle's system, often by setting out puzzles rather than final answers.

key_ideas.text: He wrote two large works on plants, the first systematic ordering of the plant world.
He questioned whether everything in nature has a purpose, pointing to things like insects that live only a day.
His Characters offers thirty short, often funny sketches of bad character types from everyday Athens.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Theophrastus as a short Socratic module. Start with Aristotle's colleague and successor at the Lyceum, c. 371–287 BCE, then his three key ideas: the first systematic study of plants; doubts about purpose everywhere in nature; the Characters, sketches of everyday types. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Alexander of Aphrodisias
thinkers.summary: Alexander of Aphrodisias was a Peripatetic philosopher active in the late second and early third century CE, and one of the heads of the philosophical schools in Athens. He wrote close commentaries on Aristotle that later commentators treated as a model. By reading Aristotle as one unified system, he helped shape the 'Aristotelianism' later attacked in early modern times.

key_ideas.text: Aristotle's philosophy is one unified whole, so apparent tensions should be smoothed over.
The human soul is the perishable form of the body, while the active intellect (the mind that is always thinking) is divine and separate.
Fate is simply the natural order of things, which leaves room for chance and for what is up to us, against Stoic determinism.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Alexander of Aphrodisias as a short Socratic module. Start with the leading ancient commentator on Aristotle, active around 200 CE, then his three key ideas: Aristotle as one unified system; the soul as the body's form and a divine active intellect; fate as nature's order, against Stoic determinism. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Epicureanism

tagline.text: A world made of atoms, and a calm life of pleasure without fear of death.

date_range: late 4th century BCE onward (featured thinkers to the 1st century BCE: Lucretius, mid-90s to mid-50s BCE; Philodemus, ca. 110–ca. 30 BCE)
description: Atomist materialism joined to an ethics of tranquil pleasure, freedom from fear of death, and gods who are unconcerned with human affairs.

questions.text: Why should I not be afraid of death?
Which pleasures actually make a life happy, and which just leave me wanting more?
If the gods don't run the world, how should I think about them?

themes.title: Atoms and the void
themes.text: Everything, the soul included, is made of tiny indivisible particles (atoms) moving through empty space. Epicurus took this picture from earlier atomists like Democritus and reworked it. Lucretius calls physics the cure for the wrong religion that stands in the way of happiness.

themes.title: Death is nothing to us
themes.text: Because the soul is made of atoms that scatter when we die, there is no afterlife and no punishment waiting. While we exist, death is not here; when death comes, we are not. Lucretius adds that we don't mind the time before we were born, so why mind the time after?

themes.title: Pleasure as calm
themes.text: The goal is happiness, understood as freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance (ataraxia, peace of mind). This is not a life of chasing thrills: empty desires like fame or great wealth can never be satisfied, so wisdom means telling desires apart.

themes.title: Friendship and community
themes.text: Epicurus valued friendship extremely highly, and Epicureans were encouraged to form communities. Philodemus wrote on how such a community should work, including the skill of frank, caring criticism among friends.

themes.title: Gods without fear
themes.text: Lucretius and Philodemus held that gods exist (scholars debate whether Epicurus himself did), but gods who live in perfect peace and take no part in running the world, neither rewarding nor punishing. Fear of angry, meddling gods is a false belief that makes people miserable.

reacted_against.text: Plato's Forms, and the belief in an immortal soul facing punishment after death, whose fear Epicurus saw as the main cause of human anxiety.

sources.section: 3.417–829: Thirty proofs of the mortality of soul

links.label: Democritus's atoms
links.reason: Epicurus inherited his atomist physics from the earlier atomists, above all Democritus, and studied under a Democritean.

links.label: Platonic Forms dropped
links.reason: Epicurus' materialism dispensed with Plato's transcendent Forms and denied that the soul survives death.

links.label: criterion of truth doubted
links.reason: The Academics questioned the Epicurean claim to a criterion of truth and defended skeptical action against Epicurean critics.

links.label: Epicureanism rejected outright
links.reason: Neoplatonists absorbed almost the whole Greek tradition except Epicureanism, which they rejected outright.

links.label: Epicureanism studied anew
links.reason: The Renaissance's renewed study of Epicureanism (with other Hellenistic schools) loosened Aristotle's hold.

thinkers.name: Epicurus
thinkers.summary: Epicurus (341–270 BCE) was an Athenian citizen raised on Samos, who studied with a follower of Democritus. After teaching on Lesbos and at Lampsacus, he returned to Athens in 307/06 and bought the property known as the Garden, which gave his school its name. He built a complete system joining atomist physics to an ethics of calm pleasure.

key_ideas.text: The goal of life is happiness: freedom from bodily pain and from mental disturbance.
Death is nothing to us: while we exist death is absent, and when death comes we no longer exist.
Some desires are natural and necessary, some natural but unnecessary, and some empty, like fame or great wealth, which can never be satisfied.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Epicurus as a short Socratic module. Start with the founder of the Garden in Athens, 341–270 BCE, then his three key ideas: happiness as freedom from pain and disturbance; death is nothing to us; the three kinds of desire. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Philodemus
thinkers.summary: Philodemus of Gadara (ca. 110–ca. 30 BCE) studied at the Epicurean school in Athens and moved to Italy, probably in the 70s BCE. He was also a poet whose verse Cicero praised. Most of his philosophy comes from papyrus rolls found in the 18th century in a villa at Herculaneum, buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE.

key_ideas.text: Anger comes in two kinds: a natural, mild pang and a destructive rage built on false beliefs.
Frank criticism is a skill: the leader of a community diagnoses friends' moral errors, like a doctor of the soul.
Music and poetry can give harmless enjoyment, but mastering their complex rules distracts from philosophy.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Philodemus as a short Socratic module. Start with an Epicurean philosopher and poet (ca. 110–ca. 30 BCE) who moved to Italy and whose books survived at Herculaneum, then his three key ideas: natural anger versus destructive rage; frank criticism as care for the soul; enjoying the arts without being swallowed by them. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Lucretius
thinkers.summary: Titus Lucretius Carus (mid-90s to mid-50s BCE) wrote On the Nature of Things (De rerum natura), a six-book Latin poem on Epicurean physics. Little is known of his life beyond what can be inferred from the poem itself. His poem is our fullest source for Epicurean atomism and our only Epicurean source for the atomic 'swerve'.

key_ideas.text: Poetry is like honey on the rim of a cup: it sweetens a teaching that only seems bitter.
The soul dies with the body, so death is nothing to fear; we feel no dread about the time before we were born.

sources.section: 3.417–829: Thirty proofs of the mortality of soul

key_ideas.text: Atoms sometimes swerve by a tiny amount, at no fixed time or place, which lets them collide and form things.

sources.section: 2.62–332: Atomic motion and the swerve (for this section, see Fowler 2002).

study_prompt.text: Teach me Lucretius as a short Socratic module. Start with the poet (mid-90s to mid-50s BCE) whose six-book Latin poem, On the Nature of Things, sets out Epicurean physics, then his three key ideas: poetry as honey on the rim of the cup; the mortal soul, and why we need not dread death any more than the time before birth; the atomic swerve. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Stoicism

tagline.text: Live in agreement with nature, because virtue is the only good.

date_range: c. 300 BCE onward (major figures through the 2nd century CE)
description: A system of physics, logic and ethics with interlocking parts, teaching that only virtue is good and that living virtuously means living in agreement with nature.

questions.text: What in my life is actually up to me?
Can I still be happy if I lose my health, money or good name?
If everything is fated, am I still responsible for what I do?

themes.title: Living in agreement with nature
themes.text: Zeno called the goal of life 'living in agreement': one consistent reason, never at war with itself. Later Stoics added 'with nature', meaning bringing your own reason in tune with the reason that runs the whole cosmos.

themes.title: Virtue is the only good
themes.text: Health, wealth and reputation are 'indifferents': worth choosing in normal life, but they never make you happier or unhappier. Only virtue, the perfected state of reason, is truly good, so happiness is in your own power.

themes.title: Emotions are judgments
themes.text: For the Stoics, passions like fear or anger are not forces that ambush us; they follow from judgments we assent to, usually false ones about what is good or bad. Change the judgment and the emotion changes. The wise person has calm 'good feelings' instead.

themes.title: Fate and what is up to us
themes.text: Everything happens through an unbreakable chain of causes, which the Stoics call fate. Yet whether we assent to an impression (how something appears to us) is up to us, and that is where responsibility lives.

themes.title: Citizens of the world
themes.text: Because all humans share reason, they are fellow citizens, together with Zeus, of one world-city (a cosmopolis). Justice therefore reaches every human being, not just your own city.

sources.section: 3. Justice: Acting for the Sake of the Cosmopolis

reacted_against.text: The Peripatetic and Academic view that 'external goods' like health and wealth add to happiness; the Stoics also competed with Epicurus's school, founded in Athens just before theirs.

links.reason: Zeno read Socratic dialogues and was influenced by Plato's Academy; Stoic psychology returns to Socrates' intellectualism.

links.label: non-rational soul rejected
links.reason: Stoic psychology rejects the Platonic-Aristotelian idea of non-rational parts of the mature soul.

links.label: Stoic certainty attacked
links.reason: Academic skeptics Arcesilaus and Carneades attacked the Stoic criterion of truth and Stoic epistemology.

links.label: Neo-Stoic revival
links.reason: Renaissance thinkers renewed the study of Stoicism; SEP calls Justus Lipsius the most important figure of the Neo-Stoic movement.

sources.section: 5.3 On Renaissance and Early Modern Philosophy

links.label: Stoic elements taken up
links.reason: Christian writers took up some elements of Stoicism.

thinkers.name: Zeno of Citium
thinkers.summary: Zeno of Citium founded the Stoic school around 300 BCE, named after the painted porch (stoa) in Athens where it met. He was a keen reader of Socratic dialogues, studied with the Cynic Crates, and was influenced by Plato's Academy. None of his works survives complete.

key_ideas.text: The goal of life is 'living in agreement': one consistent reason that is never at odds with itself.
Philosophy has three parts, physics, logic and ethics, that form one connected whole.
Some impressions are 'cognitive': the way they arise from what they show (and, on some readings, their clarity) guarantees they are true. Assenting to one he called 'cognition' (katalēpsis).

study_prompt.text: Teach me Zeno of Citium as a short Socratic module. Start with the founder of the Stoa in Athens around 300 BCE, then his three key ideas: living in agreement; philosophy as one connected whole of physics, logic and ethics; cognition, assent to an impression guaranteed to be true. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Chrysippus of Soli
thinkers.dates: head of the school c. 230–206 BCE
thinkers.summary: Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–207 BCE) was once a long-distance runner, studied under Cleanthes, and led the Stoic school from around 230 BCE. He is counted as the school's foremost theorist and systematizer. He is reported to have written over 150 works, but only fragments remain.

key_ideas.text: Everything is fated, yet assent is up to us: like a pushed cylinder that rolls because of its own shape.
The happy life and the virtuous life are one and the same.
He built a logic of whole statements (propositional logic) as an alternative to Aristotle's.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Chrysippus of Soli as a short Socratic module. Start with the Stoa's foremost theorist and systematizer, who led the school from about 230 BCE, then his three key ideas: fate and assent, the cylinder analogy; the happy life is the virtuous life; a propositional logic as an alternative to Aristotle's. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Seneca
thinkers.summary: Seneca (c. 1 BCE – 65 CE) was born in Corduba in Spain and educated in Rome. His political life was dramatic: exiled to Corsica in 41, he later became Nero's tutor and then adviser. Writing in Latin letters, essays and consolations, he shaped how later generations understood Stoicism.

key_ideas.text: Philosophy is a practice of training and healing, aimed at the person making progress rather than the perfect sage.
Emotions like anger are judgments; 'moderate emotion' makes as little sense as moderate madness.
He writes within Stoicism but independently: he follows the Stoic 'leaders' where they lead, not where they send him, and uses ideas from other schools when they help.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Seneca as a short Socratic module. Start with the Stoic from Corduba, educated in Rome, who became Nero's tutor and adviser, c. 1 BCE – 65 CE, then his three key ideas: philosophy as therapy for someone making progress; anger as a judgment, and no 'moderate' emotions; an independent Stoic who follows his leaders, not orders. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Epictetus
thinkers.summary: Epictetus was born in the 50s CE in Hierapolis and spent part of his life as the slave of Epaphroditus, an administrator at Nero's court. After gaining his freedom he lectured on his own, but was forced to leave Rome, presumably under Domitian's edict of 89 banning philosophers from Italy. He set up his own school at Nicopolis in Greece and taught there until his death around 135. According to their preface, the Discourses were written up by the historian Arrian of Nicomedia, though a few scholars think Epictetus composed them himself.

key_ideas.text: Volition (prohairesis, our power to choose) is the true self, and nothing outside can force it.
Body, possessions and reputation are 'externals', neither good nor bad in themselves; what counts is how we use them.
Grief, fear and envy come from the false belief that happiness lies outside us; correct the judgment and the feeling changes.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Epictetus as a short Socratic module. Start with a former slave who became a Stoic teacher at Nicopolis and died around 135 CE, then his three key ideas: volition as the free, true self; externals and how we use them; correcting judgments to change feelings. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Marcus Aurelius
thinkers.summary: Marcus Aurelius was born in 121 CE and ruled Rome as emperor from 161 until his death in 180, through wars, rebellions and plague. Part of his Meditations, notes written to and for himself, dates from his last military campaigns. Stoic teachers shaped him, and Epictetus is the Stoic author he singles out.

key_ideas.text: Only virtue is good and only vice bad; most of what we worry about is indifferent to our happiness.
Live as a citizen of the cosmic city, working for the good of all human beings.

sources.section: 3. Justice: Acting for the Sake of the Cosmopolis

key_ideas.text: Keep Stoic truths at hand in short sayings, like 'Erase impressions!', to stay free of pain and fear.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Marcus Aurelius as a short Socratic module. Start with the Stoic Roman emperor of 161–180 CE who wrote the Meditations, then his three key ideas: only virtue is good; citizenship of the cosmic city; short sayings as reminders. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Ancient Skepticism

tagline.text: Suspend judgment and keep investigating, rather than claim how things really are.

description: Academic and Pyrrhonian skeptics who suspended judgment and kept investigating, rather than asserting how things really are.
debatable: Two movements (Academic and Pyrrhonian) under one node; SEP treats them in one entry.

questions.text: Can I ever be sure that the way something looks to me is true?
Can I live and act without firm beliefs?
Could giving up the hunt for certainty bring me peace of mind?

themes.title: Suspending judgment
themes.text: The skeptics' key move is epochē (suspension of judgment): neither affirming nor denying a claim once you have weighed it. 'Skeptic' originally just meant inquirer, someone who keeps investigating.

sources.section: 3.2 What is the Skeptical ability or skill?

themes.title: No sure test of truth
themes.text: The Stoics claimed some impressions are so clear they cannot be false. The Academic skeptics replied that a false impression could always look just the same, and called into question whether there is any test of truth (a 'criterion'). Carneades instead offered the persuasive as a guide.

themes.title: Arguing both sides
themes.text: Skeptics trained themselves to set an equally strong argument against every argument. Carneades is said to have argued for justice one day in Rome and against it the next.

sources.section: 3.2 What is the Skeptical ability or skill?

themes.title: Peace of mind
themes.text: Pyrrhonian skeptics aimed at tranquility (ataraxia). Troubled by conflicting appearances, they hoped to settle what is true, found the arguments balanced, suspended judgment, and found calm followed.

themes.title: Living by appearances
themes.text: Critics said a person without beliefs could not act. Skeptics answered that you can be guided by what appears to you, or by what is persuasive, without claiming it is true.

reacted_against.text: The 'dogmatists', especially the Stoics, who claimed that certain impressions give a sure test of truth; Arcesilaus thought Zeno far too confident about our powers of knowing.

links.label: Socratic questioning
links.reason: Socrates' commitment to examination as the way to find out inspired the skepticism of the Hellenistic Academy.

links.label: Stoic certainty attacked
links.reason: Academic skeptics Arcesilaus and Carneades attacked the Stoic criterion of truth and Stoic epistemology.

links.label: criterion of truth doubted
links.reason: The Academics questioned the Epicurean claim to a criterion of truth and defended skeptical action against Epicurean critics.

links.label: ancient skepticism revived
links.reason: Renaissance skepticism was inspired by the revival of ancient Greek skepticism, notably the rediscovery of Sextus Empiricus (1562).

sources.section: 5.1 Augustine: Re-Conceiving Skepticism in a Theological Framework

links.label: skeptical tools against dogma
links.reason: Enlightenment thinkers used skeptical tropes drawn from the ancient skeptics to attack traditional dogmas.

links.label: knowledge defended against skeptics
links.reason: In Contra Academicos Augustine defended knowledge against the Academic skeptics.

sources.section: 5.1 Augustine: Re-Conceiving Skepticism in a Theological Framework

thinkers.name: Pyrrho
thinkers.summary: Pyrrho of Elis lived from around 365–360 to around 275–270 BCE and is said to have travelled with Alexander the Great to India. He wrote nothing; much of what we know comes through his follower Timon. Later Pyrrhonist skeptics took him as their inspiration, though he may not have been a skeptic in their sense.

key_ideas.text: According to Timon's report, to be happy one must ask three things: what are things like by nature, how should we relate to them, and what follows?
Things are indifferent, unstable and indeterminate (or, on another reading, we cannot tell them apart), so we should not trust our perceptions and beliefs.
Living without opinions leads first to speechlessness and then to tranquility.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Pyrrho as a short Socratic module. Start with a philosopher from Elis, c. 365/60–275/70 BCE, who inspired the Pyrrhonist skeptics, then his three key ideas: three questions for a happy life, as Timon reports them; things as indeterminate, and not trusting perceptions; tranquility through living without opinions. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Arcesilaus
thinkers.summary: Arcesilaus became head of Plato's Academy and turned it skeptical, inspired by Socrates the examiner. Like Socrates, he wrote nothing. He was a sharp critic of the Stoics' theory of knowledge, and his attacks pushed Chrysippus to reshape Stoicism.

key_ideas.text: Examine someone's view using their own premises, as Socrates did.
Any impression could be matched by a false one that looks the same, so there is no test of truth and we should suspend judgment about everything.
A skeptic can still act, guided by perception without adding belief, like walking through a door without judging 'here is the door'.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Arcesilaus as a short Socratic module. Start with the head of Plato's Academy in the 3rd century BCE who turned it skeptical, then his three key ideas: the Socratic dialectical method; no criterion of truth, so suspend judgment; acting without belief. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Carneades
thinkers.summary: Carneades was born in Cyrene in North Africa, studied in Athens at the Academy and with the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon, and became head of the Academy. In 156/5 BCE he went to Rome on an embassy, where he is said to have argued for justice one day and against it the next. He wrote nothing, but his ideas shaped the Academy until its end.

key_ideas.text: Act on the persuasive, and test important impressions harder, like poking a coiled rope in a dark room to check it isn't a snake.
On the traditional reading, arguing for and against justice was meant to show that its defenders lack the arguments they think they have.
He mapped every possible view about the goal of life, apparently using the map to challenge the Stoics.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Carneades as a short Socratic module. Start with the head of the Academy, born in Cyrene, who on an embassy to Rome is said to have argued for justice one day and against it the next, then his three key ideas: the persuasive, tested in stages; arguing both sides of justice; a map of all views on life's goal. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Sextus Empiricus
thinkers.summary: Sextus Empiricus was a Pyrrhonian skeptic who probably lived in the second or third century CE; his name comes from the Empirical school of medicine. Almost nothing is known of his life. His Outlines of Pyrrhonism is the fullest account of Pyrrhonian skepticism we have.

key_ideas.text: Skepticism is a skill: setting equally convincing arguments against each other until judgment is suspended.

sources.section: 3.2 What is the Skeptical ability or skill?

key_ideas.text: Tranquility comes after suspending judgment, not by aiming straight at it.
Skeptics keep investigating, unlike dogmatists who claim to have found the truth and Academics who say it cannot be found.

sources.section: 3.1 What do Skeptics do, and where do they get their name?

study_prompt.text: Teach me Sextus Empiricus as a short Socratic module. Start with a Pyrrhonian skeptic of probably the 2nd or 3rd century CE, linked to the Empirical school of medicine, then his three key ideas: skepticism as a skill of balanced opposition; tranquility following suspension of judgment; skeptics as people still investigating. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Neoplatonism

tagline.text: A late Platonism that derives all of reality from one first principle, the One.

description: A late-antique Platonism deriving all reality from a single first principle, the One.
debatable: The name is modern; its members called themselves simply Platonists (SEP).

questions.text: How could a whole, varied universe come from one single source?
If everything flows from the Good, where does evil come from?
If I am more than my body, what is my life really for?

themes.title: The One beyond being
themes.text: Everything depends on a single first principle, called the One or the Good. It is so simple and so far beyond ordinary things that almost nothing can be said about it, except that it is absolute unity.

themes.title: Unfolding in stages
themes.text: Reality emerges from the One as a hierarchy of levels, eternally rather than step by step in time: first Intellect (pure consciousness), then Soul, then the living world. Each level then turns back toward its source, a pattern they called procession and return.

themes.title: Mind before matter
themes.text: They held that consciousness comes first and the physical world is its outer effect. Matter is the faint edge where this outflow runs out, like darkness at the end of light.

themes.title: Climbing back to the divine
themes.text: The goal of life is to return the divine in us to its source. Plotinus and Porphyry trusted philosophy for this climb, while Iamblichus and Proclus gave priority to theurgy (sacred rites held to be established by the gods themselves).

themes.title: Harmonising the whole tradition
themes.text: These Platonists tried to weave nearly all earlier Greek thought, myth and religion into one system. Porphyry argued that Plato and Aristotle agree on essentials, and Proclus sought harmony between old religious revelations and Plato.

sources.section: 3.4.3 The Harmony of Plato and Aristotle

reacted_against.text: It rejected the materialism of the Epicureans and the Stoics' view that everything real is a body, and Plotinus vehemently opposed Gnosticism.

links.label: Plato as highest authority
links.reason: The Neoplatonists called themselves Platonists and held Plato's views above all others; Plotinus took Plato as having laid the fundamentals.

links.label: Aristotle's Metaphysics as starting point
links.reason: Plotinus used passages of Aristotle's Metaphysics as starting points, and his sessions read commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.

links.label: Epicureanism rejected outright
links.reason: Neoplatonists absorbed almost the whole Greek tradition except Epicureanism, which they rejected outright.

links.label: Platonist frame for Aristotle
links.reason: Medieval Aristotelianism was transmitted in a Platonist context; via Augustine and Pseudo-Dionysius, Neoplatonism shaped Aquinas and Scotus.

sources.section: 1.2 The Platonic Schools of Late Antiquity

links.label: Plato and Plotinus revived
links.reason: Ficino's translations of Plato and Plotinus led a dramatic Renaissance revival of Neoplatonism.

links.label: Platonism for Christian faith
links.reason: At Milan Augustine met Neoplatonically inclined Christians who showed him a philosophically informed Christianity; through him and the Greek Fathers, Neoplatonism shaped Christian theology.

thinkers.name: Plotinus
thinkers.summary: Plotinus was born in Egypt, studied with Ammonius Saccas in Alexandria and taught in Rome from 244 until his death in 270. He is usually seen as the founder of Neoplatonism. His pupil Porphyry gathered his writings into the Enneads (six sets of nine treatises).

key_ideas.text: All reality comes from the One, or the Good, a first principle beyond being itself.

sources.section: 7. The First Principle of Everything: the One, or the Good

key_ideas.text: Reality unfolds in levels (the One, Intellect, Soul), and each level is drawn back toward the Good by love.

sources.section: 7. The First Principle of Everything: the One, or the Good

key_ideas.text: Evil comes from below, not above: it arises when souls turn their attention toward matter instead of the higher world.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Plotinus as a short Socratic module. Start with a philosopher born in Egypt who taught in Rome from 244 until his death in 270 and is usually seen as the founder of Neoplatonism, then his three key ideas: everything comes from the One, beyond being; reality unfolds in levels and returns to the Good through love; evil comes from turning toward matter. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 7. The First Principle of Everything: the One, or the Good

thinkers.name: Porphyry
thinkers.summary: Porphyry was born in Tyre in Phoenicia, studied with Longinus in Athens and then with Plotinus in Rome, whose Platonism he adopted. He edited Plotinus' Enneads and wrote the Isagoge, for centuries the standard introduction to logic. He also defended vegetarianism, partly as a matter of justice toward animals.

key_ideas.text: Plato and Aristotle agree on the essentials, even where they differ in detail.

sources.section: 3.4.3 The Harmony of Plato and Aristotle
1.2 The Platonic Schools of Late Antiquity

key_ideas.text: His Isagoge sorted how we classify things (genus, species, difference, property, accident) and became the standard way into logic for centuries.

sources.section: 3.4.4 The Isagoge, Universals and the Acquisition of Concepts

key_ideas.text: Philosophy, not ritual, is what saves the higher, thinking part of the soul.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Porphyry as a short Socratic module. Start with a pupil of Plotinus, born in Tyre, who edited his teacher's Enneads, then his three key ideas: Plato and Aristotle agree on essentials; the Isagoge as the gateway to logic; philosophy, not ritual, saves the higher, thinking part of the soul. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Iamblichus
thinkers.summary: Iamblichus was a Syrian Neoplatonist, probably a student of Porphyry, and is sometimes called the second founder of Neoplatonism. He shaped the later system of the Athenian school. He criticised Plotinus sharply, took a darker view of the human soul and championed salvation through ritual.

key_ideas.text: The human soul descends fully into the body and cannot rise on its own; it needs help from the gods.
Theurgy, meaning sacred ritual done together with the gods, is the soul's main path to salvation, ahead of pure reasoning.
Mathematics, studied in the Pythagorean way, is a purifying and uplifting spiritual exercise.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Iamblichus as a short Socratic module. Start with a Syrian Neoplatonist of the late 3rd and early 4th century CE, probably a student of Porphyry, then his three key ideas: the soul fully descends and needs the gods' help; theurgy (ritual with the gods) as the way to salvation; mathematics as a purifying exercise. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Proclus
thinkers.summary: Proclus led the Platonic school in Athens for almost fifty years and was the most authoritative philosopher of late antiquity. He wrote commentaries on Plato, Aristotle and Euclid and systematic works across philosophy. He played a crucial role in passing Platonism on to the Middle Ages.

key_ideas.text: His Elements of Theology sets out his metaphysics step by step, starting from the One as the ultimate cause, as a chain of proved propositions.
The old Greek myths and religious revelations can be shown to agree with the philosophy of Pythagoras and Plato.
The gods know future events without fixing them, because how something is known depends on the knower, not the thing known.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Proclus as a short Socratic module. Start with the head of the Platonic school in Athens (412–485), then his three key ideas: his metaphysics set out step by step from the One; harmony between old religions and Plato; divine foreknowledge without fixing our choices. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Early Christian Philosophy (Patristic)

tagline.text: Early Christian thinkers who used Greek philosophy, above all Platonism, for faith.

date_range: c. 185 – c. 525/6 CE (Origen's birth to Boethius's death)
description: The Church Fathers and their heirs, who used Greek philosophy, above all Platonism, to think through Christian faith.
debatable: Where this group ends and medieval philosophy begins is unsettled: by some chronologies, Augustine himself founded the medieval Latin tradition (SEP).

questions.text: If God is good and made everything, where does evil come from?
If God already knows what I will do, am I still free?
Should I believe first and understand later, or the other way round?

themes.title: Greek philosophy serving faith
themes.text: These Christian thinkers used Greek philosophy, above all Platonism, as a tool for explaining scripture and doctrine. Philosophy was a respected helper, but scripture had the final word.

themes.title: Faith seeking understanding
themes.text: Belief comes first in time, but understanding is the goal. Reason is a gift to be used to grasp what one already accepts in faith, not a rival to it.

themes.title: Evil as missing goodness
themes.text: Evil is not a thing or substance in its own right but a lack or corruption of goodness. Everything that is real is good in its degree, because God created it.

themes.title: Speaking of a God beyond words
themes.text: God is greater than any name we can give. One can praise God with names, but in the end every name, and even every denial, has to be left behind.

themes.title: Foreknowledge and freedom
themes.text: If God knows everything in advance, can people still choose? Boethius answered that God sees all of time at once, as one eternal present, so his knowing does not force our choices.

reacted_against.text: It pushed back against dualist and Gnostic views that blamed evil on a rival power or a split within God, and against skeptics who said truth cannot be known.

links.reason: At Milan Augustine met Neoplatonically inclined Christians who showed him a philosophically informed Christianity; through him and the Greek Fathers, Neoplatonism shaped Christian theology.

thinkers.name: Origen
thinkers.summary: Origen was a Christian scholar from Alexandria who wrote commentaries on scripture and made heavy use of allegory. Though later considered a heretic, he laid the foundations of philosophical theology for the church. He was taught by an Ammonius whom most scholars identify with Plotinus' teacher.

key_ideas.text: Scripture has deeper meanings beneath the literal words, which allegorical reading brings out.
God is not a body but bodiless mind, even when scripture calls him fire or spirit.
Souls stay free in their choices; misusing that freedom is what leaves a soul captive to the devil, and he expected most souls to be purified after death.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Origen as a short Socratic module. Start with a Christian scholar from Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) who laid foundations for philosophical theology, then his three key ideas: reading scripture allegorically; God as bodiless mind; free souls, captivity through misused freedom, and purification. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Augustine of Hippo
thinkers.summary: Augustine was born in Roman North Africa, followed the Manichean religion for nine years, and was won over to Christianity partly through reading the Platonists. He was perhaps the greatest and most influential Christian philosopher of antiquity. His Confessions is a philosophy written from the first person.

key_ideas.text: Faith comes first, and reason then works to understand what faith accepts.
Evil is not a substance but a lack or corruption of good.
Since the fall, humans cannot will the good by their own effort; only God's grace frees the will.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Augustine of Hippo as a short Socratic module. Start with a Christian philosopher born in Roman North Africa (354–430), perhaps the greatest and most influential Christian philosopher of antiquity, then his three key ideas: faith seeking understanding; evil as a lack of good; grace freeing the will. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
thinkers.dates: wrote late 5th or early 6th c. (between 485 and 518–28 CE)
thinkers.summary: Pseudo-Dionysius was a Christian Neoplatonist who carried pagan Neoplatonism, especially Proclus, into a new Christian setting. He wrote under the name of Dionysius, a first-century convert of St Paul, which gave his works near-apostolic authority. Modern scholars think he most probably studied with Proclus.

key_ideas.text: Every name for God must finally be denied, and then the denials too must be left behind.
Names like over-good and over-being praise God as one while showing God's many sides.
Angels and the church are ordered in ranked hierarchies through which the vision of God is passed down.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite as a short Socratic module. Start with a Christian Neoplatonist of the late 5th or early 6th century who wrote under the name of a first-century convert of St Paul, then his three key ideas: denying every name for God; the over-names that praise God; hierarchies of angels and church. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Boethius
thinkers.summary: Boethius was a Roman aristocrat who translated Aristotle's logic into Latin and wrote commentaries and textbooks on it. Accused of treason, he was imprisoned and probably executed in 526, and in prison he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy. He became, with Augustine and Aristotle, a basic author for the Latin Middle Ages.

key_ideas.text: Riches, status, power and pleasure are fortune's goods of little worth; the true goods are the virtues and sufficiency, and since he has lost none of them, his fall need not cut him off from true happiness.

sources.section: 5. The Consolation of Philosophy: The Argument of Books I–V.2

key_ideas.text: God lives in an eternal present and knows all times at once, so his foreknowledge does not force our choices.
His Latin translations of Aristotle's logic remained standard throughout the Middle Ages, and his commentaries were the main way logicians of the 9th–12th centuries understood Aristotle.

Start with a Roman aristocrat and scholar (c. 475/7–526?) who wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison, then his three key ideas: fortune's goods versus true goods; God's eternal present and our freedom; his Latin translations of Aristotle's logic, standard through the Middle Ages. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Scholasticism

tagline.text: Medieval university philosophy that joined Aristotle with Christian theology.

date_range: flourishing from the 12th-century Paris schools onward, to perhaps around 1700
description: University philosophy of the Latin Middle Ages, reconciling Aristotle's newly recovered works with Christian theology by commentary and disputation.
debatable: SEP ties it to a method: Aquinas epitomises the scholastic method of the newly founded universities. Its end date is open; SEP calls around 1700 a plausible end for medieval philosophy, and this style of university philosophy ran on for at least three centuries after the mid-1300s.

questions.text: Can reason prove that God exists, or must I take it on faith?
When I call two cats 'cats', is there a real catness they share, or just a word?
If a pagan philosopher's argument seems sound, can it clash with what faith teaches?

themes.title: Aristotle in the university
themes.text: As Aristotle's full works reached Latin Europe, the new universities built their arts teaching around him. Thinkers worked out how this pagan philosopher fitted with Christian teaching.

themes.title: Reasoning through authorities
themes.text: Much philosophy was done as commentary on respected texts, which often led to new ideas. Abelard's method of reconciling texts that seem to contradict each other, by careful analysis of concepts, became the basis of later theology.

themes.title: Faith seeking understanding
themes.text: Faith was the starting point, and reason was used to understand it more deeply. Several thinkers offered proofs that God exists, from Anselm's ontological argument to Aquinas' arguments from a first cause.

themes.title: The problem of universals
themes.text: Is there something real, like humanity, shared by Socrates and Plato, or only a shared word or concept? Scotus said yes, there is a real common nature; Abelard and Ockham said no.

themes.title: Will, freedom and God's choices
themes.text: Later thinkers stressed God's free will and power. Scotus made God's will the ground of good and evil and saw human freedom as having real options at the very moment of choice; Ockham followed him on God's will.

reacted_against.text: Abelard answered both those who wanted no reasoning in matters of faith and those he called pseudo-dialecticians, who took reason to be the final judge of everything, even matters of faith.

links.label: Aristotle rediscovered
links.reason: Thirteenth-century university philosophers were enthused by newly available Aristotle; Aquinas worked to write commentaries on all of Aristotle's principal works.

links.reason: Medieval Aristotelianism was transmitted in a Platonist context; via Augustine and Pseudo-Dionysius, Neoplatonism shaped Aquinas and Scotus.

links.reason: Augustine's works were read widely in the Middle Ages and gave philosophers a source and inspiration.

thinkers.name: Anselm
thinkers.summary: Saint Anselm of Canterbury was the outstanding Christian philosopher and theologian of the eleventh century. He is best known for the ontological argument for God's existence in his Proslogion. He also wrote on God's nature and on human freedom, sin and redemption.

key_ideas.text: Faith seeking understanding: an active love of God that seeks to know God more deeply.

sources.section: 2.1 “Faith Seeking Understanding”: The character and purpose of Anselm’s theistic proofs

key_ideas.text: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and such a being must really exist.
Freedom is the power to keep a right will for its own sake, not the power to sin.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Anselm as a short Socratic module. Start with the outstanding Christian philosopher and theologian of the 11th century, then his three key ideas: faith seeking understanding; God as that than which nothing greater can be thought; freedom as keeping a right will. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Peter Abelard
thinkers.summary: Peter Abelard was the leading philosopher and theologian of the twelfth century, a famous teacher, poet and musician. He is arguably the greatest logician of the Middle Ages and the first great nominalist (someone who denies that universals are real things). His affair with Héloïse made him a tragic figure of romance, and his clash with Bernard of Clairvaux over reason and religion made him a hero of the Enlightenment.

key_ideas.text: Universals are not things in the world but words; only individual things exist.
Only the agent's intention decides whether an action is good or bad; deeds in themselves are morally neutral.
Apparently contradictory authoritative texts can be reconciled through careful analysis of their concepts.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Peter Abelard as a short Socratic module. Start with the leading philosopher, theologian and logician of the twelfth century, then his three key ideas: universals are only words; intention decides moral worth; reconciling clashing authorities by analysis. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Thomas Aquinas
thinkers.summary: Thomas Aquinas was a Dominican friar from near Aquino in Italy who studied in Paris and Cologne. He was the greatest figure in philosophy and theology of thirteenth-century Europe and epitomises the method of the new universities. He took inspiration from Aristotle and built a new system from it.

key_ideas.text: Natural reason can prove that God exists, for example by showing there must be a first cause.
What reason truly demonstrates cannot contradict Christian teaching, though some truths are known only by revelation.
Natural law is the way rational beings take part in God's eternal law, and it grounds morality.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Thomas Aquinas as a short Socratic module. Start with a Dominican friar (c. 1225–1274) who epitomises the method of the new universities and built a new system inspired by Aristotle, then his three key ideas: proving God through a first cause; reason and faith cannot truly clash; natural law as the root of morality. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: John Duns Scotus
thinkers.summary: John Duns Scotus was born in a Scottish village and became an Oxford Franciscan who was later sent to teach at Paris. His subtle thought earned him the nickname the Subtle Doctor. He shaped debates on religious language, universals and human freedom. He absorbed Aristotle but thought Aristotle's God left no room for divine choice.

sources.section: 1.1 The life of John Duns the Scot

key_ideas.text: Pure perfections, like goodness, are said of God and creatures in the very same sense; the difference is one of degree, with God having them infinitely.

sources.section: 2.3 Divine infinity and the doctrine of univocity

key_ideas.text: Things share real common natures, and each individual is made itself by its thisness (haecceity).
True freedom means having real alternatives at the very moment of choice.

study_prompt.text: Teach me John Duns Scotus as a short Socratic module. Start with a Franciscan born in Scotland (1263/66–1308) and nicknamed the Subtle Doctor, then his three key ideas: words for pure perfections, like goodness, mean the same for God and us; common natures and thisness; freedom as real options in the moment. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: William of Ockham
thinkers.summary: William of Ockham was a Franciscan, born in the village of Ockham in Surrey, who worked at Oxford and London and later fled a papal investigation to the court of Ludwig of Bavaria. He is probably best known today for nominalism, and the principle called Ockham's Razor is named after him. He also wrote on logic, natural philosophy, knowledge, ethics and politics.

key_ideas.text: Ockham's Razor: don't believe in more kinds of things than reason, experience or scripture require.
There are no universal things; only universal concepts and words, applied to similar individual things.
The pope is not above correction, and a heretical pope may even be removed with help from secular rulers.

study_prompt.text: Teach me William of Ockham as a short Socratic module. Start with a Franciscan (c. 1287–1347) after whom Ockham's Razor is named, then his three key ideas: Ockham's Razor; only concepts and words are universal; limits on the pope's power. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.
