name: Renaissance Philosophy

tagline.text: A return to Greek and Roman sources, ethics and eloquence, against scholastic logic.

description: A return to classical Greek and Roman sources and to ethics and eloquence, with humanists setting themselves against scholastic logic and university learning.
debatable: IEP's 'Renaissance Philosophy' has humanism as one current beside Renaissance Aristotelianism, Platonism (Ficino) and revived Hellenistic schools; the node covers them all.

questions.text: What good is philosophy if it doesn't help me live a better life?
Should I trust the textbooks, or go back and read the original sources myself?
Given how limited we are, can we know anything for certain at all?

themes.title: Back to the sources
themes.text: Thinkers prized ancient Greek and Roman texts and read them in the original languages. Close study of language became a tool for criticism, as when Valla exposed a forged document and Erasmus edited the Greek New Testament.

themes.title: Philosophy for living well
themes.text: Humanists cared most about moral philosophy and wrote for a general audience. Their aim was to make people and cities more virtuous, not to solve technical puzzles.

themes.title: Persuasion over formal logic
themes.text: Humanists mocked the logic taught in universities. Valla and others wanted arguments judged by how well they persuade and work in real debate, with logic serving rhetoric.

themes.title: Plato reborn
themes.text: Platonism returned as a rival to Aristotle. Ficino translated Plato and Plotinus, and Platonists read the dialogues as sacred mysteries and saw philosophy as a way toward union with God.

themes.title: Old schools, new life
themes.text: Stoicism, Epicureanism and Skepticism were revived. Petrarch drew on Stoic remedies for distress, Valla built a Christian ethics of pleasure, and skeptical arguments were used in religious debates.

reacted_against.text: It reacted against scholastic Aristotelian philosophy, its technical logic and the university education built on it, which humanists saw as useless for living well.

links.label: scholastic logic condemned
links.reason: Petrarch set out what became the standard critique of scholastic philosophy, and fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century humanists condemned university education and scholastic logic.

links.label: Plato and Plotinus revived
links.reason: Ficino's translations of Plato and Plotinus led a dramatic Renaissance revival of Neoplatonism.

links.label: Neo-Stoic revival
links.reason: Renaissance thinkers renewed the study of Stoicism; SEP calls Justus Lipsius the most important figure of the Neo-Stoic movement.

sources.section: 5.3 On Renaissance and Early Modern Philosophy

links.label: Epicureanism studied anew
links.reason: The Renaissance's renewed study of Epicureanism (with other Hellenistic schools) loosened Aristotle's hold.

links.label: ancient skepticism revived
links.reason: Renaissance skepticism was inspired by the revival of ancient Greek skepticism, notably the rediscovery of Sextus Empiricus (1562).

sources.section: 5.1 Augustine: Re-Conceiving Skepticism in a Theological Framework

thinkers.name: Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)
thinkers.summary: Petrarch was one of the founding figures of the humanist movement. He set out what became the standard humanist critique of scholastic philosophy and turned philosophy back toward the classical tradition and ethics. He influenced later humanists such as Salutati, Bruni and Bracciolini.

key_ideas.text: Scholastic philosophy is useless if it does not help us live a good life.
It is foolish to cling to a single authority, since all authorities can be wrong.
Stoic ideas, drawn from Seneca and Cicero, can serve as therapy against emotional distress.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch) as a short Socratic module. Start with a 14th-century founder of the humanist movement, then his three key ideas: philosophy must help us live well; no single authority deserves blind trust; Stoic remedies for distress. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Lorenzo Valla
thinkers.summary: Lorenzo Valla was one of the most important humanists of his time and the author of a famous handbook of Latin style. He used his command of classical languages to criticise ideas and institutions. He exposed the Donation of Constantine as a forgery and compared Jerome's Latin Bible with the Greek New Testament.

key_ideas.text: Careful study of language and history can expose forgeries, such as the document behind the papacy's claim to rule lands.
Philosophy should fit common sense and ordinary language, so he cut Aristotle's categories down to three: substance, quality and action.
Christian love and blessedness can be understood as a kind of pleasure, using Epicurean ideas against Stoic virtue.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Lorenzo Valla as a short Socratic module. Start with a leading humanist (c. 1406–1457) who used classical languages to criticise ideas and institutions, then his three key ideas: language as a tool to expose forgeries; philosophy in ordinary language; a Christian ethics of pleasure. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Marsilio Ficino
thinkers.summary: Marsilio Ficino was one of the most famous philosophers of the Italian Renaissance and its most important Platonist. He translated all of Plato's works into Latin, and also Plotinus, writing commentaries along the way. He blended philosophical, religious and literary traditions.

sources.section: 2.3 The Complete Works of Plato and the place of translation

key_ideas.text: True wisdom was handed down through an ancient theology, a chain of inspired sages in which Plato was a key link.
The human soul is immortal and longs to return to its divine origin, like a pilgrim seeking home.
Love flows from God into all things and binds them together.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Marsilio Ficino as a short Socratic module. Start with the most important Platonist of the Italian Renaissance (1433–1499), who translated all of Plato into Latin, then his three key ideas: the ancient theology of inspired sages; the immortal soul longing for home; love binding all things. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 2.3 The Complete Works of Plato and the place of translation

thinkers.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
thinkers.summary: Giovanni Pico was a prince fully committed to philosophy and strikingly original. In 1486 he published 900 Conclusions for a public debate in Rome, but the pope halted it and legal proceedings followed. He is famous today for a speech, later titled the Oration on the Dignity of Man, that he never delivered.

key_ideas.text: In his Oration, God tells Adam he alone can make himself what he wants; yet the goal Pico sets is to become angel-like and finally merge with God.
He built a Christian Kabbalah (a reading of Jewish mystical teaching), even claiming magic and Kabbalah proved Christ's divinity.
He used the study of texts and history to attack astrology's claim to ancient wisdom, and restated older arguments that it cannot reliably predict.

sources.section: 2.5 Being and the One and Astrology

study_prompt.text: Teach me Giovanni Pico della Mirandola as a short Socratic module. Start with a prince and philosopher (1463–1494) known for his 900 Conclusions and his Oration, then his three key ideas: what the Oration really asks of us; Christian Kabbalah; his attack on astrology's claim to ancient wisdom. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 2.5 Being and the One and Astrology

thinkers.name: Desiderius Erasmus
thinkers.summary: Erasmus of Rotterdam was the most important Christian humanist, combining Christian faith with classical learning. He edited the Greek New Testament and wrote The Praise of Folly. He favoured peace and compromise in the Reformation debates, but broke with Luther over Luther's sectarianism, and the two also clashed in a polemic over free will.

key_ideas.text: Return to the sources: read scripture in its original languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin.
The philosophy of Christ: learned piety and simple devotion matter more than scholastic speculation.
Against Luther, the human will is very weak but, with God's grace, can still choose the path of salvation.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Desiderius Erasmus as a short Socratic module. Start with Erasmus of Rotterdam (c. 1466 or 1469–1536), a Christian humanist, then his three key ideas: back to scripture in its original languages; the philosophy of Christ; a weak but free will, helped by grace. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Rationalism

tagline.text: Reason, not only the senses, is a key source of what we know.

description: The view that reason, independent of sense experience, is a key source of knowledge and concepts, some of them innate.
debatable: 'Continental Rationalists' is a later grouping, first applied by Kant, and SEP says such schemes should be used only with great caution.

questions.text: Is there anything I can know with no room at all for doubt?
Are some ideas already in my mind before experience teaches me anything?
Does everything that happens have a reason why it is so and not otherwise?

themes.title: Reason over the senses
themes.text: Some knowledge comes from reason alone, not from the senses, and it is better than sense knowledge. For Descartes, what reason grasps is certain while the senses always leave some doubt.

themes.title: Ideas we are born with
themes.text: Some concepts or truths are part of our rational nature from the start, and experience only triggers our awareness of them. Descartes counted the idea of God as innate; Leibniz compared the mind to marble whose veins shape the statue.

themes.title: Intuition and deduction
themes.text: Knowledge is built like geometry: from truths seen directly by the mind (intuition), more truths are drawn out step by step (deduction). Rationalists claimed this works even for truths about God and the world.

themes.title: Systems from first principles
themes.text: Big systems were built from a few basic principles. Spinoza derived his Ethics step by step from definitions and axioms, and Leibniz rested his on principles such as sufficient reason.

themes.title: Mind and body
themes.text: How do thinking and the physical world fit together? Descartes made them two separate substances, Spinoza two sides of one Nature, and Leibniz a harmony set up in advance by God.

reacted_against.text: It reacted against the scholastic Aristotelian view that all knowledge comes through the senses, which Descartes called a childhood prejudice.

links.label: scholastic assumptions attacked
links.reason: Descartes attacked the assumptions of the scholastic Aristotelians that stood in the way of the new science.

links.label: innate knowledge rejected
links.reason: Empiricists reject innate knowledge; Locke spends the whole first book of his Essay arguing against it.

links.label: Descartes as pillar, then Kant's limits
links.reason: Descartes' rationalist system, with its method of doubt, is one of the pillars of Enlightenment thought. Then: Kant's early work was enmeshed in Leibniz-Wolff rationalism, until Hume shook his faith in its assumption that metaphysical knowledge is possible.

sources.section: b. Dogmatic Slumber, Synthetic A Priori Knowledge, and the Copernican Shift

links.label: Cartesian certainty rejected
links.reason: The pragmatists set out to overcome Cartesianism, rejecting Descartes' individualist search for certainty.

links.label: Descartes' first-person turn
links.reason: Husserl credited Descartes with the decisive first-person turn (his Cartesian Meditations), while rejecting most Cartesian doctrines.

sources.section: 3. The transcendental turn: Epoché, phenomenological reduction, and transcendental idealism

thinkers.name: René Descartes
thinkers.summary: René Descartes was a first-rank mathematician, an important scientist and an original metaphysician. He developed the techniques that made algebraic geometry possible and pictured nature as matter obeying a few universal laws. His view of an immaterial mind linked to the brain gave rise to the modern mind–body problem.

key_ideas.text: Use skeptical arguments to doubt the senses, and even reasoning, in order to find what is truly certain.
Even while doubting, I cannot doubt that I exist as a thinking thing, and what I perceive very clearly and distinctly is true.

sources.section: 3.2 The mark of truth and the circle

key_ideas.text: Mind (whose essence is thought) and body (whose essence is extension in space) are two distinct substances.

study_prompt.text: Teach me René Descartes as a short Socratic module. Start with a first-rank mathematician, scientist and metaphysician (1596–1650), then his three key ideas: doubting the senses, and even reasoning, to find certainty; the thinking self and clear and distinct perception; mind and body as distinct substances. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Baruch Spinoza
thinkers.summary: Baruch Spinoza grew up in Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish community and was expelled from it in 1656. He is among the most radical philosophers of the early modern period. His naturalistic views on God and the human being ground an ethics of mastering the passions, a democratic politics and a critique of sectarian religion.

key_ideas.text: There is only one substance, God or Nature, and everything else exists in it.
Everything, including our will, is fully determined by causes; there is no free will in the usual sense.
We find freedom and happiness by understanding our passions and so reducing their hold on us.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Baruch Spinoza as a short Socratic module. Start with a philosopher (1632–1677) who grew up in Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish community and was expelled from it in 1656, then his three key ideas: one substance, God or Nature; everything is determined; freedom through understanding the passions. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
thinkers.summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz is known as the last universal genius, working in metaphysics, logic, mathematics, physics, law and history. He held that the only truly real things are simple, mind-like substances he called monads. He answered the mind–body problem with a harmony set up in advance by God.

sources.section: 5.1 Monads and the World of Phenomena

key_ideas.text: Nothing happens without a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise.
God always acts for the best, so this is the best of all possible worlds.
The mind is not a blank slate but like veined marble: innate ideas shape what it can know.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz as a short Socratic module. Start with the thinker known as the last universal genius (1646–1716), then his three key ideas: the principle of sufficient reason; the best of all possible worlds; the mind as veined marble. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Empiricism

tagline.text: All our ideas and knowledge come, in the end, from experience.

description: The view that all our concepts and knowledge come ultimately from experience, not innate ideas.
debatable: 'British Empiricists' is likewise a later historians' grouping (SEP).

questions.text: If I wasn't born with ideas, where does everything in my mind come from?
Why do I expect the future to be like the past?
If experience is my only source of knowledge, are there things I simply cannot know?

themes.title: The blank slate
themes.text: The mind starts empty and experience writes on it. Locke said all our basic ideas come from sensation (the senses) and reflection (noticing our own mental acts).

themes.title: No innate ideas
themes.text: Empiricists denied that any knowledge or concepts are inborn. Locke argued that if they were, children would know them, and they don't.

themes.title: Ideas are copies
themes.text: Hume held that every simple idea is a fainter copy of an earlier impression (a vivid feeling or perception). So experience also sets the limits of what our ideas can mean.

themes.title: Knowing the limits
themes.text: Before reaching for answers, we should check what our minds can handle. Some things we may never know, and belief should match the evidence.

themes.title: Cause and habit
themes.text: We never see a necessary link between cause and effect, only one thing regularly following another. Hume concluded that our idea of causation comes from a habit of expectation.

reacted_against.text: It reacted against the rationalist claim that some knowledge and ideas are innate, part of the mind before any experience.

links.label: innate knowledge rejected
links.reason: Empiricists reject innate knowledge; Locke spends the whole first book of his Essay arguing against it.

links.label: Locke, then Kant's answer to Hume
links.reason: The rise of empiricism is characteristic of the period; Locke's Essay is a foundational Enlightenment text. Then: Hume's skepticism woke Kant from his 'dogmatic slumber'; the critical philosophy was designed as an answer to Hume.

sources.section: b. Dogmatic Slumber, Synthetic A Priori Knowledge, and the Copernican Shift

links.label: Hume on utility
links.reason: Hume is an early precursor; Bentham found virtue equated with utility in Hume's Treatise and borrowed the term from him.

links.label: experience, made radical
links.reason: James presented pragmatism as the empiricist attitude in a more radical form.

links.label: empiricism rebuilt with logic
links.reason: Logical positivists (Vienna Circle): the Vienna Circle set out to reconceive empiricism using modern logic and science.

thinkers.name: John Locke
thinkers.summary: John Locke was a British philosopher, Oxford academic and medical researcher. His Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) is one of the first great defences of modern empiricism and maps the limits of what we can know. In politics he argued that sovereignty lies with the people, and in his Letter Concerning Toleration he called for the separation of Church and State.

key_ideas.text: There are no innate ideas or principles; there is no good evidence for them.
The mind begins as a blank slate, and all our basic ideas come from sensation and reflection.
Legitimate government rests on natural rights and the consent of the people, through a social contract.

study_prompt.text: Teach me John Locke as a short Socratic module. Start with a British philosopher, Oxford academic and medical researcher (1632–1704), then his three key ideas: no innate ideas; the mind as a blank slate filled by experience; government resting on natural rights and the consent of the people. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: George Berkeley
thinkers.summary: George Berkeley was an Irish-born philosopher and Bishop of Cloyne, and a sharp critic of Descartes, Malebranche and Locke. He is famous for idealism, the view that reality consists only of minds and their ideas. He also wrote on vision, mathematics, physics and religion, and influenced Hume and Kant.

key_ideas.text: Ordinary objects are collections of ideas, and it makes no sense for them to exist unperceived.
We cannot form abstract general ideas by stripping away particular features, as Locke often seems to suggest.
Since our sensory ideas are not caused by matter or by ourselves, they must come from another spirit: God.

study_prompt.text: Teach me George Berkeley as a short Socratic module. Start with an Irish-born philosopher and Bishop of Cloyne (1685–1753), then his three key ideas: ordinary objects are ideas and cannot exist unperceived; no abstract general ideas; God as the cause of our perceptions. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: David Hume
thinkers.summary: David Hume was a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment who applied the experimental method of the sciences to philosophy. He is famous for his skepticism, his naturalism and his challenges to religion. In his own time he was better known for his histories and essays.

key_ideas.text: All simple ideas are fainter copies of earlier impressions (vivid perceptions and feelings).
Reason cannot serve as the foundation of our expectation that the future will be like the past; custom or habit drives it.
Moral judgments come from feeling: we call a trait virtuous because viewing it gives us a particular pleasure.

study_prompt.text: Teach me David Hume as a short Socratic module. Start with a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment (1711–1776), better known in his day for his histories and essays, then his three key ideas: ideas as copies of impressions; our expectations about the future rest on habit, not reason; morality grounded in feeling. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: The Enlightenment and Kant

tagline.text: Trust in reason and science to question authority, ending in Kant's limits of reason.

date_range: 18th century (roots in the 16th–17th-century scientific revolution; Kant's Critique 1781; ends roughly with the 1790s)
description: A movement of confidence in reason and science to question traditional authority, ending in Kant's critical philosophy, which tested what reason itself can know.
debatable: A period and movement, not a school; it spans rationalists, empiricists and skeptics. Kant is merged in here (decision L17); SEP's Kant entry places his Critique at the Enlightenment's end (§2.1), while IEP's German Idealism entry names him among that movement's most famous figures.

questions.text: Why should I let a church, a king or tradition tell me what to believe, if I can work it out for myself?
If science explains nature with fixed laws, where do my freedom and my morals fit in?

sources.section: 1.4 Science of Man and Subjectivism in the Enlightenment

questions.text: How far can human reason really reach, and where does it run out?

themes.title: Think for yourself
themes.text: Kant described enlightenment as growing out of a self-imposed immaturity: being unable to use your own understanding without someone else steering. Across the movement this meant trusting your own reason and experience over tradition, myth and prejudice.

themes.title: Science as the model
themes.text: The success of the new science, above all Newton's, made people confident that reason could understand nature and improve human life. Philosophy stopped being theology's servant and became an independent force that could challenge the old and build the new.

themes.title: Questioning church and crown
themes.text: Enlightenment thinkers found that political and social authority often rested on religious myth and obscure tradition. Most attacked superstition, fanaticism and church power rather than religion as such, and many hoped for a purified, 'rational' religion.

themes.title: Gathering all knowledge
themes.text: The Encyclopedia, edited by Diderot and d'Alembert and published from 1751 to 1772, tried to collect human knowledge and pass it on to improve society. It was secular and quietly anti-authoritarian, so the French state censored it.

sources.section: 1.2 Ascendance as Writer and Philosophe through the Encyclopédie (1750–1765)

themes.title: Rights, consent and the social contract
themes.text: The period shaped the idea of government by consent of the governed, the ideals of freedom and equality, basic individual rights and religious toleration. Rousseau offered a contrasting model built on the general will, the will of citizens aimed at their common good.

sources.section: 3.1 The idea of the general will

reacted_against.text: The authority of tradition, the established church and absolute monarchy, and the superstition, prejudice and myth that were seen as competing with each person's own reason and experience.

links.label: Descartes as pillar, then Kant's limits
links.reason: Descartes' rationalist system, with its method of doubt, is one of the pillars of Enlightenment thought. Then: Kant's early work was enmeshed in Leibniz-Wolff rationalism, until Hume shook his faith in its assumption that metaphysical knowledge is possible.

links.label: Locke, then Kant's answer to Hume
links.reason: The rise of empiricism is characteristic of the period; Locke's Essay is a foundational Enlightenment text. Then: Hume's skepticism woke Kant from his 'dogmatic slumber'; the critical philosophy was designed as an answer to Hume.

links.label: skeptical tools against dogma
links.reason: Enlightenment thinkers used skeptical tropes drawn from the ancient skeptics to attack traditional dogmas.

links.label: Kant's idealism radicalised
links.reason: Fichte, Schelling and Hegel radicalised Kant's transcendental idealism into absolute idealism.

links.label: Helvétius and Beccaria
links.reason: Bentham found the utility principle in the writings of Hume, Helvétius and Beccaria; SEP places Helvétius in the radical French Enlightenment.

links.label: Kant's thing in itself rejected
links.reason: Peirce used the pragmatic maxim against Kant's 'thing in itself' and judged Kant's logic shallow.

links.label: Kant's synthetic a priori banned
links.reason: Logical positivists (Vienna Circle): the Circle banned Kant's synthetic a priori as refuted by the progress of science.

links.label: reason turned domination
links.reason: Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment traces how Enlightenment reason became instrumental and an instrument of domination.

thinkers.name: Voltaire
thinkers.summary: Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie d'Arouet, a French writer and public activist who did much to define the Enlightenment. He wrote plays, stories and poems as well as philosophy, and championed Newton's science against the grand systems of Descartes and Leibniz. From the 1750s he campaigned publicly against what he called fanaticism and superstition.

key_ideas.text: No authority, however sacred, should be shielded from questioning by critical reason.
Science should describe and measure what we can observe, and leave out speculation about what cannot be seen (metaphysics).
Free speech and thought are worth defending, though the famous 'defend to the death your right to say it' line is not actually his.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Voltaire as a short Socratic module. Start with the French writer and activist (1694–1778) who did much to define the Enlightenment, then his three key ideas: no authority, however sacred, is above questioning by critical reason; science should describe and measure what we can observe and leave out metaphysics; free speech and thought are worth defending. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
thinkers.summary: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712 and wrote on politics, education and human psychology, as well as composing music and writing novels. His central worry was how people can stay free when they depend more and more on each other, and on each other's opinion. He was often a dissenting voice within the Enlightenment, and his stress on feeling made him a forerunner of Romanticism.

key_ideas.text: People are good by nature but are corrupted by society, though what that natural goodness means is hard to pin down.
A legitimate state is guided by the general will: laws that come from all citizens and apply equally to all.

sources.section: 3.1 The idea of the general will

key_ideas.text: Education should follow the child's natural growth and let the child discover things, rather than impose lessons by authority.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Jean-Jacques Rousseau as a short Socratic module. Start with the Geneva-born writer on politics and education (1712–1778), often a dissenting voice within the Enlightenment, then his three key ideas: people are good by nature but corrupted by society; a legitimate state is guided by the general will, laws that come from all and apply to all; education should follow the child's natural growth rather than impose lessons by authority. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Denis Diderot
thinkers.summary: Denis Diderot was, with Voltaire, a leader of the French philosophes after 1750, and with d'Alembert he edited the Encyclopédie, meant to change the common way of thinking. In 1749 his writings got him jailed for three months in Vincennes prison. He did philosophy through plays, novels and art criticism as well as essays, and SEP calls him arguably the most sophisticated of the philosophes.

key_ideas.text: Knowledge should be gathered and shared as a living engine for changing what we know, not as a dusty record.

sources.section: 1.2 Ascendance as Writer and Philosophe through the Encyclopédie (1750–1765)

key_ideas.text: We learn about nature through experiment and observation, not by abstract reasoning alone.
There is only one kind of stuff, matter, always in flux; living beings are temporary clusters of it (materialism).

study_prompt.text: Teach me Denis Diderot as a short Socratic module. Start with the co-editor of the Encyclopédie (1713–1784), arguably the most sophisticated of the French philosophes, then his three key ideas: knowledge should be shared as an engine for changing what we know; we learn about nature through experiment and observation, not abstract reasoning alone; there is only one kind of stuff, matter, always in flux (materialism). Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Immanuel Kant
thinkers.summary: Immanuel Kant was born in 1724 in Königsberg, then capital of East Prussia, and SEP calls him the central figure in modern philosophy. His Critique of Pure Reason (1781) came near the end of the Enlightenment and tested what reason itself can and cannot know. The core idea running through his work is human autonomy, which literally means giving the law to yourself.

key_ideas.text: We know the world only as it appears to us, shaped by our mind's own forms such as space and time, never as things are in themselves.
Morality comes from reason: act only on a rule you could will as a law for everyone (the categorical imperative, a duty that binds whatever you happen to want).
Enlightenment means thinking for yourself rather than letting others think for you.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Immanuel Kant as a short Socratic module. Start with the philosopher born in Königsberg (1724–1804) whose Critique of Pure Reason came near the Enlightenment's end, then his three key ideas: we know the world only as it appears to us, never as things are in themselves; act only on a rule you could will as a law for everyone (the categorical imperative); enlightenment means thinking for yourself. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: German Idealism

tagline.text: Systems after Kant that derive everything from one first principle, the absolute.

description: Fichte, Schelling and Hegel radicalised Kant into absolute idealism, building complete systems derived from a single first principle, the absolute.

questions.text: Is there anything out there that my mind could never, even in principle, know?
Could one single starting point explain everything, from logic to art to politics?
How can I be free if I am also part of a nature run by causes?

themes.title: From Kant to absolute idealism
themes.text: Kant held that we know only appearances, not things in themselves. Fichte, Schelling and Hegel went further: a thing that could never be an object for consciousness, they argued, is a contradiction in terms.

themes.title: One system for everything
themes.text: The idealists wanted one system covering logic, metaphysics, ethics, politics and art. Fichte, Schelling and Hegel tried to derive it all from a single first principle, called the absolute (the unconditioned starting point).

themes.title: Becoming a self through others
themes.text: Fichte argued that you become a self only when another free person calls on you to respect their freedom. Hegel built on this: self-consciousness depends on mutual recognition, and patterns of recognition make up social life.

themes.title: Nature and art
themes.text: Schelling treated nature as a living, productive whole that includes us, not just matter obeying laws. He held that art can reveal what philosophy cannot turn into an object of knowledge, a view Hegel later disputed.

themes.title: Spirit learning through history
themes.text: Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit follows a series of ways of seeing the world, each breaking down on its own contradictions and giving rise to the next. Its story maps onto Western history from the Greeks to his own day.

reacted_against.text: The limits Kant had placed on knowledge, especially his unknowable things in themselves, and the old split between rationalism and empiricism.

links.label: Kant's idealism radicalised
links.reason: Fichte, Schelling and Hegel radicalised Kant's transcendental idealism into absolute idealism.

links.label: Hegel's history inverted
links.reason: Marx took over Hegel's teleological account of history and 'inverted' it into a materialist theory, appropriating many Hegelian ideas.

links.label: Hegel's system rejected
links.reason: Kierkegaard's attack on detached theory was aimed mainly at Hegel's system; Schelling's critique of Hegel reached him too.

links.label: break with absolute idealism
links.reason: Moore and Russell broke away from absolute idealism, and Hegel became a main target of the founders of analytic philosophy.

links.label: Hegel's method of critique
links.reason: Hegel has been a continual reference point, his method used as a model of immanent critique.

thinkers.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
thinkers.summary: Johann Gottlieb Fichte came from a poor family of ribbon weavers in Saxony, and reading Kant in 1790 changed his thinking. His Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation (1792) appeared without his name and was hailed as Kant's own, which made him famous once the truth came out. At the University of Jena (1794–1799) he built a system he called the Wissenschaftslehre ('Doctrine of Scientific Knowledge'), grounded on the 'pure I' (the bare self).

key_ideas.text: Philosophy must start either from the free self or from things; Fichte started from freedom, since theory alone cannot settle the choice.

sources.section: 3. The Starting Point of the Jena Wissenschaftslehre

key_ideas.text: A thing that is not an object for our consciousness makes no sense, so even Kant's 'thing in itself' is posited by the mind.
You become a self only when another free person calls on you to respect their freedom, so mutual recognition is part of selfhood.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Johann Gottlieb Fichte as a short Socratic module. Start with the philosopher from a poor Saxon family (1762–1814) who built his Wissenschaftslehre at Jena, then his three key ideas: philosophy must start from the free self or from things, and he chose freedom; even Kant's thing in itself is posited by the mind; you become a self only through mutual recognition. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

sources.section: 3. The Starting Point of the Jena Wissenschaftslehre

thinkers.name: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling was, with Fichte and Hegel, one of the three most influential German Idealists. He changed his views so often that he has been called a philosophical Proteus, yet SEP stresses that he was often an impressively rigorous logical thinker. He is remembered for his philosophy of nature, his view that the thinking self is never fully transparent to itself, and his later critique of Hegel.

key_ideas.text: Nature is not dead matter but a productive whole that includes us, and conscious mind grows out of it.
Subject and object, mind and world, must at root be one, or knowledge could never connect them (his 'identity philosophy').
Pure thought cannot capture real existence on its own, which is why he criticized Hegel's complete system.

sources.section: 5. Positive and Negative Philosophy, and the Critique of Hegel

study_prompt.text: Teach me Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von Schelling as a short Socratic module. Start with the German Idealist (1775–1854) remembered for his philosophy of nature, the self that is never fully transparent to itself, and his critique of Hegel, then his three key ideas: nature is a living, productive whole from which mind emerges; mind and world are at root the same; pure thought cannot capture real existence, against Hegel. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: G. W. F. Hegel
thinkers.summary: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, born in Stuttgart in 1770, studied alongside Hölderlin and Schelling and became the most systematic of the German Idealists. After the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) he went on to celebrity in Berlin, where he died in 1831. He is perhaps best known for seeing history as purposeful development, an idea Marx later turned into a materialist theory.

key_ideas.text: Thought moves forward through contradiction: each way of seeing the world breaks down and gives rise to a fuller one.
I become aware of myself as a subject only through mutual recognition with other subjects.
Freedom is realized in shared social life ('ethical life'), where individuals, families, civil society and the state come together; he contrasted this with abstract right and morality.

study_prompt.text: Teach me G. W. F. Hegel as a short Socratic module. Start with the most systematic German Idealist (1770–1831), perhaps best known for seeing history as purposeful development, then his three key ideas: thought moves forward as each way of seeing the world breaks down and gives rise to a fuller one; I become aware of myself as a subject only through mutual recognition; freedom is realized in ethical life, where families, civil society and the state come together. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Utilitarianism

tagline.text: The right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness.

date_range: 1789 (Bentham's Principles) – late 19th century (Sidgwick); refined since, often under the name consequentialism
description: The moral theory that right actions are those that produce the greatest happiness.

questions.text: Is an action right or wrong simply because of what it leads to?
Does my own happiness count for more than a stranger's?
What good does this law or custom actually do?

themes.title: Consequences decide
themes.text: Utilitarianism is a kind of consequentialism: whether an act or policy is right depends entirely on its results. Bentham even valued liberty only for what it brings about, not for its own sake.

themes.title: Pleasure and pain
themes.text: For the classical utilitarians, the good to be produced is pleasure and the bad is pain. Bentham called pleasure and pain our two 'sovereign masters', ruling all we do, say and think.

themes.title: Everyone counts the same
themes.text: Utilitarianism is impartial: one person's happiness counts no more than anyone else's. Sidgwick put it as the good of any one person mattering no more, from the point of view of the universe, than anyone else's.

themes.title: A tool for reform
themes.text: Godwin, Bentham and Mill were all concerned with legal and social reform. Their main motive was to see useless, corrupt laws and social practices changed, and for that they needed a moral theory they could use as a critical tool. Bentham, a jurist, gave his own career to law reform and to social and political improvement.

themes.title: Higher and lower pleasures
themes.text: Mill broke with Bentham by arguing that pleasures differ in quality as well as amount. The better pleasure is the one preferred by people who have experienced both.

reacted_against.text: Laws and customs defended by tradition or appeals to nature, legal 'fictions' or mere disgust, rather than by their real effects on people's happiness.

links.label: Hume on utility
links.reason: Hume is an early precursor; Bentham found virtue equated with utility in Hume's Treatise and borrowed the term from him.

links.label: Helvétius and Beccaria
links.reason: Bentham found the utility principle in the writings of Hume, Helvétius and Beccaria; SEP places Helvétius in the radical French Enlightenment.

sources.section: 1.4 Science of Man and Subjectivism in the Enlightenment

thinkers.name: Jeremy Bentham
thinkers.summary: Jeremy Bentham was a jurist and political reformer, the philosopher most tied to the founding of modern utilitarianism. He gave the theory its secular, systematic form, especially in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (printed 1780, published 1789). He wrote on law, punishment, prisons, economics, education and democracy, aiming at a complete legal code based on utility.

key_ideas.text: Pleasure and pain govern us, and the right action is the one that tends to increase happiness.
A pleasure or pain can be weighed by its intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fruitfulness, purity and how many people it reaches (the 'felicific calculus').
Laws should be judged only by the harm or good they do, so mere dislike of a practice is no reason to punish it.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Jeremy Bentham as a short Socratic module. Start with the jurist and reformer (1748–1832) who founded systematic utilitarianism, then his three key ideas: pleasure and pain govern us, and right acts increase happiness; pleasures and pains can be weighed (the felicific calculus); laws should be judged by harm and good, not by dislike. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: John Stuart Mill
thinkers.summary: John Stuart Mill was, according to SEP, the most influential English-language philosopher of the nineteenth century: a naturalist, a utilitarian and a liberal. His father, an ally of Bentham, gave him an intensely demanding education; at twenty Mill suffered a mental crisis and found relief in Romantic poetry. His major works include On Liberty (1859) and Utilitarianism (1861).

key_ideas.text: Some pleasures, such as those of the mind, are higher in quality than merely bodily ones.
The only good reason for society to interfere with someone's liberty is self-protection, and he defended this on utilitarian grounds.

sources.section: 4.5 On Liberty and Freedom of Speech

key_ideas.text: Discrimination against women harms overall happiness; he likened the marriage law of his day to slavery.

sources.section: 4.4 Equality, the Sexes, and the Nineteenth Century

Start with the nineteenth-century naturalist, utilitarian and liberal (1806–1873), author of On Liberty, then his three key ideas: some pleasures, such as those of the mind, are higher in quality than bodily ones; the only good reason for society to interfere with someone's liberty is self-protection; discrimination against women harms overall happiness. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Henry Sidgwick
thinkers.summary: Henry Sidgwick spent his whole career at Cambridge, and in 1869 resigned his fellowship because he could no longer in conscience affirm the Church of England's articles. His The Methods of Ethics (1874) in many ways marked the culmination of classical utilitarianism, and some have called it the best treatise on moral theory ever written. He also worked on economics, politics, education and psychical research.

key_ideas.text: Everyday moral reasoning mixes three methods, egoism, intuited rules and utilitarianism, and he argued utilitarianism is the most basic.
From the point of view of the universe, no one's good matters more than anyone else's.
Reason seems to back both self-interest and the general good, and he could not fully reconcile them (the 'dualism of practical reason').

study_prompt.text: Teach me Henry Sidgwick as a short Socratic module. Start with the Cambridge philosopher (1838–1900) whose Methods of Ethics in many ways marked the culmination of classical utilitarianism, then his three key ideas: everyday moral reasoning mixes three methods, and utilitarianism is the most basic; from the point of view of the universe, no one's good matters more than anyone else's; reason seems to back both self-interest and the general good (the dualism of practical reason). Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Marxism

tagline.text: A materialist theory of history and a critique of capitalism.

description: Marx's materialist theory of history and critique of capitalism: alienation, class struggle, ideology and the case for communism.
debatable: Also a political movement; here only the philosophical tradition.

questions.text: Why does my work so often feel as if it isn't really mine?
Do ideas drive history, or do economics and material life drive our ideas?
Why do unequal societies stay so stable, and could things be organized differently?

themes.title: Alienation
themes.text: Alienation means being cut off from something that properly belongs to you. Marx argued that workers under capitalism are separated from what they make, from their own activity, from each other and from their human nature.

themes.title: Historical materialism
themes.text: Societies rise and fall as they first help and then hold back human productive power. A society's economic structure shapes its politics, law and ideas, rather than the other way round.

themes.title: Class and exploitation
themes.text: History moves through a series of economic systems marked by class struggle. Marx traced capitalist profit to surplus value taken from workers, though whether his idea of exploitation must depend on his labour theory of value is debated.

sources.section: 5.1 Production and class, base and superstructure

themes.title: Ideology and false appearances
themes.text: Some widely shared beliefs may hide how society really works, helping class-divided societies stay stable. Lukács later argued that capitalism makes social relations look like relations between things.

themes.title: People remake their world
themes.text: Marx combined materialism with the idealists' stress on human activity: people transform their world through material work, not just thought. Lukács framed Marxism as a self-conscious transformation of society.

reacted_against.text: German idealism, which Marx and Engels said mistook ideas for real things, and the capitalist society of their day.

links.label: Hegel's history inverted
links.reason: Marx took over Hegel's teleological account of history and 'inverted' it into a materialist theory, appropriating many Hegelian ideas.

links.label: Marxism revised and updated
links.reason: The Frankfurt School revised and updated Marxism, taking Marx as the model of radical critique.

links.label: Marx read structurally
links.reason: The poststructuralists worked with structuralist readings of Marx; Foucault took up Marx through Althusser.

thinkers.name: Karl Marx
thinkers.summary: Karl Marx is often seen mainly as a revolutionary, but he was trained as a philosopher, with a doctorate in ancient philosophy, and engaged closely with Hegel. His work covers human nature and alienation, a theory of history, a critique of capitalism, ideology, the state and a predicted communist future. He was famously reluctant to sketch communism in detail, holding that history itself would deliver its basic structure.

key_ideas.text: Under capitalism work is alienated: workers are separated from their products, their activity, each other and their own human nature.
A society's economic structure explains its politics, law and ideas, and when it holds back productive power it is overturned.
Religion is the 'opium of the people', a comforting illusion that will fade once material life is freed.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Karl Marx as a short Socratic module. Start with the philosopher and revolutionary (1818–1883) who engaged closely with Hegel, then his three key ideas: work under capitalism is alienated, separating workers from their products, activity, each other and their nature; the economic structure shapes society and is overturned when it holds back productive power; religion is a comforting illusion that will fade once material life is freed. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Engels
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Engels was Marx's lifelong collaborator, a leading figure in early socialist politics and a self-taught writer on history, science and philosophy. He wrote The Condition of the Working-Class in England (1845) and co-wrote The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto (1848) with Marx. He called himself Marx's 'second fiddle', but SEP stresses his originality, and how far his views differ from Marx's is still debated.

sources.section: 1.1 Early work and collaboration with Marx

key_ideas.text: Materialism means being comes before thinking and nature before mind, and he applied this well beyond economic history.
Nature itself is historical, always in process; he saw Darwin's work as a parallel to what Marx did for society.
Family and kinship belong to society's material base, alongside economic production.

sources.section: 5.3 Late revisions: Women and the family

Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Georg Lukács
thinkers.summary: Georg (György) Lukács was a literary theorist and philosopher born in Budapest, widely seen as a founder of 'Western Marxism' and a forerunner of critical theory. He joined the Hungarian Communist Party in 1918 and served in the revolutionary government of 1919. He is best known for The Theory of the Novel (1916) and History and Class Consciousness (1923).

key_ideas.text: Under capitalism the commodity form spreads to everything, so social relations come to look like relations between things (reification).
Workers are placed to understand society as a whole better than the bourgeoisie, though they must achieve it (an early 'standpoint theory').
Art reflects objective reality, but unlike science it shows it through human inner experience.

sources.section: 4.4 Aesthetics: Realism and the Work of Art as a Closed Totality

Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

name: Existentialism

tagline.text: Philosophy that starts from the single person who must choose how to live.

date_range: roots in the 19th century (Kierkegaard, Nietzsche); movement in mid-20th-century France
description: Philosophy that starts from concrete, first-person human existence: freedom, anxiety, authenticity and the search for meaning. It includes Camus's philosophy of the absurd, though Camus rejected the existentialist label.
debatable: Absurdism is folded in: SEP files Camus's 'absurdity' among existentialist themes (§5.1), but Camus denied being an existentialist (SEP Camus, §1). SEP treats Kierkegaard and Nietzsche as nineteenth-century pioneers who laid its groundwork (intro).

questions.text: If nothing hands me a purpose, how do I live?

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity
1. The Paradoxes of Camus’s Absurdist Philosophy

questions.text: Am I living my own life, or just doing what everyone else does?
What do I do with the anxiety of being free to choose?

themes.title: Existence before essence
themes.text: No fixed human nature decides who we are; we turn up first and define ourselves through our choices. Sartre gave this its famous slogan, yet we still face given facts such as our body and our history.

themes.title: Freedom and anxiety
themes.text: Anxiety shows me that I alone must answer for whatever I choose among my possibilities. Kierkegaard called it the dizziness of freedom, and the existentialists ask us to face it rather than flee.

sources.section: 2. Kierkegaard’s Analysis of Human Existence: Despair, Social Critique, and Anxiety

themes.title: Authenticity versus the crowd
themes.text: We tend to drift along with Kierkegaard's 'public' or Nietzsche's 'herd', living by borrowed norms. Sartre and Beauvoir call this kind of self-deception 'bad faith': denying either our freedom or the facts of our situation.

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity

themes.title: Meaning without guarantees
themes.text: Nietzsche diagnosed nihilism, the loss of any overarching purpose once belief in God collapsed. Camus called the clash between our hunger for meaning and a silent universe 'the absurd', though he denied being an existentialist.

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity
1. The Paradoxes of Camus’s Absurdist Philosophy

themes.title: My freedom needs yours
themes.text: Existentialist ethics starts from the idea that no moral order is given in advance. But Beauvoir and Sartre argued that willing my own freedom commits me to willing the freedom of others.

sources.section: 5. The Ethics of Ambiguity: Bad Faith, the Appeal, the Artist

reacted_against.text: Philosophy's detached 'view from nowhere' and all-explaining systems like Hegel's, and the loss of meaning in a secular, mass, bureaucratic modern world.

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity

links.label: Hegel's system rejected
links.reason: Kierkegaard's attack on detached theory was aimed mainly at Hegel's system; Schelling's critique of Hegel reached him too.

links.label: Husserl's method applied
links.reason: Heidegger took up his teacher Husserl's phenomenological maxim 'to the things themselves'; Husserl is named among the movement's groundwork.

links.label: the decentred subject
links.reason: Existentialism's critique of foundations and grand narratives, and Nietzsche and Heidegger in particular, shaped Derrida and Foucault.

links.label: Beauvoir's Second Sex
links.reason: Beauvoir, a major existentialist, wrote The Second Sex (1949), the groundbreaking work feminist philosophers turn back to.

thinkers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
thinkers.summary: Søren Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813 and wrote mostly in the 1840s, across philosophy, theology, psychology and social critique. He opposed building grand systems and is often called the 'father of existentialism', though SEP warns the label hides as much as it shows. He has often been cast as Hegel's great opponent, but recent scholars think his main target was certain Danish Hegelians.

key_ideas.text: A self is not something you simply have but something you must become, by holding together what is given and what is possible.

sources.section: 2. Kierkegaard’s Analysis of Human Existence: Despair, Social Critique, and Anxiety

key_ideas.text: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom: being drawn to and repelled by our own possibilities.

sources.section: 2. Kierkegaard’s Analysis of Human Existence: Despair, Social Critique, and Anxiety

key_ideas.text: Life can be lived in different spheres, the aesthetic, the ethical and the religious, each finding value in a different way.

sources.section: 3. The “Spheres of Existence” or “Stages on Life’s Way”

Start with the Copenhagen writer (1813–1855) often called the father of existentialism, then his three key ideas: the self is a task to become; anxiety is the dizziness of freedom; life can be lived in aesthetic, ethical and religious spheres. Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and cultural critic who published intensively in the 1870s and 1880s. He is famous for fierce attacks on traditional European morality and religion, often by exposing the hidden psychology behind received ideas. He also proposed new values he hoped would renew culture, and SEP's existentialism entry counts him among the movement's nineteenth-century pioneers.

key_ideas.text: 'God is dead': belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, so the morality built on it is set to collapse.
Imagine living your life over and over forever; on one influential reading, your reaction tests how much you value your life (eternal recurrence).

sources.section: 6.3 The Eternal Recurrence of the Same

key_ideas.text: There is no view from nowhere: all knowing happens from perspectives, and using many of them brings us closer to objectivity.

study_prompt.text: Teach me Friedrich Nietzsche as a short Socratic module. name: Pragmatism

tagline.text: Make ideas clear by asking what practical difference they make.

description: An American philosophy that clarifies ideas by their practical consequences and treats inquiry and truth in terms of action.

questions.text: What difference would it actually make if this idea were true?
Can I hold beliefs without being certain and still make progress?
If knowledge grows from solving real problems, how should we learn and live together?

themes.title: Meaning lies in practical effects
themes.text: Peirce's pragmatic maxim says that the meaning of an idea is the practical effects we would expect if it were true. James used the same test to dissolve disputes: if neither side would make any practical difference, the quarrel is idle.

themes.title: Truth tied to inquiry and use
themes.text: Peirce saw truth as the opinion that inquirers would ultimately agree on. James called true whatever proves good to believe, and Rorty later said there is little of substance to say about truth at all.

themes.title: Fallible, not skeptical
themes.text: Pragmatists rejected Descartes' method of doubting everything at once. We can be wrong, but further inquiry can find and correct our errors, so we should be fallibilists (people who accept they may be wrong) rather than skeptics.

themes.title: Inquiry as problem-solving
themes.text: Peirce described inquiry as the struggle to replace doubt with settled belief. Dewey saw it as turning an unsettled, problematic situation into a settled one.

themes.title: Philosophy for social life
themes.text: A second generation, shaped by Dewey and his friend Jane Addams, turned pragmatism toward politics, education and social improvement. For Dewey, democracy was a whole way of living together, and schools were places to practise it.

reacted_against.text: Descartes-style philosophy that seeks certainty by doubting everything, and the picture of knowledge as a mind mirroring an outside world.

links.label: experience, made radical
links.reason: James presented pragmatism as the empiricist attitude in a more radical form.

links.label: Cartesian certainty rejected
links.reason: The pragmatists set out to overcome Cartesianism, rejecting Descartes' individualist search for certainty.

links.label: Kant's thing in itself rejected
links.reason: Peirce used the pragmatic maxim against Kant's 'thing in itself' and judged Kant's logic shallow.

links.label: Quine's pragmatist themes

thinkers.name: Charles Sanders Peirce
thinkers.summary: Charles Sanders Peirce, born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, founded American pragmatism, later calling his version 'pragmaticism' to set it apart from James's and Dewey's. He earned his living for 32 years at the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey but saw logic and scientific philosophy as his true calling. He wrote on an enormous range of subjects, from mathematics and astronomy to psychology and economics.

key_ideas.text: To make an idea clear, consider the practical effects you would expect from its object; those effects are its whole meaning (the pragmatic maxim).
Truth is the opinion that everyone who investigates would ultimately agree on.
Science works by abduction (guessing a hypothesis that explains a surprise), then deduction of what should follow, then induction (testing).

thinkers.name: William James
thinkers.summary: William James worked across physiology, psychology and philosophy; his Principles of Psychology (1890) gave us the 'stream of thought'. A close friend of Peirce, he developed and popularized pragmatism, notably in his book Pragmatism (1907), based on lectures given in 1905–1907. He also wrote on religion in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902).

key_ideas.text: A dispute that makes no practical difference either way is idle; pragmatism is a method for settling such disputes.
True ideas are those that prove good to believe and help us get into satisfactory relation with the rest of our experience.
When a choice is forced and momentous and the evidence is not in, we may have a 'right to believe', since belief can help bring about what it believes.

thinkers.name: John Dewey
thinkers.summary: John Dewey was, with Peirce and James, one of pragmatism's founders and arguably the most prominent American intellectual of the first half of the twentieth century. He wrote on ethics, logic, metaphysics, art and religion, and his ideas on education had global reach, while his writings on democracy shaped debates for decades. He preferred to call his view 'cultural naturalism', set within a Darwinian picture of living beings in their environments.

key_ideas.text: Inquiry starts from a feeling that something is amiss and, by framing a problem, forming hypotheses and testing them, turns an unsettled situation into a settled one.
Children learn best by actively working on real problems, not by passively receiving what others know.
Democracy is more than voting: it is a way of living together and sharing experience.

thinkers.name: Richard Rorty
thinkers.summary: Richard Rorty developed a distinctive and controversial pragmatism and helped spark its revival from the 1970s, often called neopragmatism. In Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979) he attacked the idea of knowledge as the mind mirroring an outside world. He set out to combine Dewey, Hegel and Darwin, though many pragmatist scholars dispute his readings of Dewey and Peirce and even his right to the label.

key_ideas.text: Knowledge is not the mind mirroring the world, and philosophy should drop that picture.
There is little of substance to say about truth; we test vocabularies by how well they help us reach our goals.
A liberal ironist knows her deepest descriptions are contingent, and holds that cruelty is the worst thing we do.

themes.title: Enlightenment turned against itself
themes.text: Horkheimer and Adorno argued that reason, meant to free us from fear, narrowed into instrumental reason (working out means without asking about ends). Pushed far enough, it becomes a new kind of domination.

themes.title: The culture industry
themes.text: Mass culture, they argued, is not made by the masses but manufactured like any other product. Standardised entertainment turns culture into a commodity and helps keep things as they are.

themes.title: Reason in conversation
themes.text: Habermas, of the second generation, looked for reason in everyday communication. His public sphere is a space where equals debate shared concerns and are moved by the better argument.

reacted_against.text: It reacted against 'traditional', positivist theory that treats the social order as a given fact, and it revised Marxism, since the workers Marx expected to bring change had turned toward fascism instead.

thinkers.summary: Horkheimer led the Frankfurt School as director of the Institute for Social Research, from 1930 and again after the war, steering it through exile mainly in America. His 1930s essays shaped the school's method, and he co-wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment with Adorno.

key_ideas.text: Critical theory, unlike traditional theory, reflects on its own place in society and aims to end injustice.

key_ideas.text: The public sphere is where private people come together to reason about matters of common concern.

name: Post-structuralism

tagline.text: French thought that questions stable meaning, the self-present subject and foundations.

description: French thought that grew out of structuralism to question stable meaning, the self-present subject and claims to foundations, through deconstruction and genealogy.
debatable: This app draws on the SEP entries on Postmodernism, Foucault and Derrida. The Postmodernism entry says its French thinkers are often called 'poststructuralists', though individually they may resist common affiliation, and the Foucault entry links him with both the structuralist and post-structuralist movements.

questions.text: Am I really the author of my own thoughts, or am I shaped by structures I never chose?
Do the categories we treat as natural, like 'normal' or 'mad', have a history?
Do the big pairs we think in, like essence and appearance or speech and writing, quietly rank one side above the other?

themes.title: Decentring the subject
themes.text: The self is not the fixed starting point of truth and knowledge. It is shaped in advance by history, language and social practices, in ways we are never fully aware of.

themes.title: Genealogy: no pure origins
themes.text: Following Nietzsche, Foucault traced how ideas and institutions arose from accidents and conflicts rather than from one clean origin. Showing this history loosens the hold of what seems natural.

themes.title: Power and knowledge
themes.text: Foucault argued that modern knowledge and control are tied together. Exams, for instance, both find out the truth about people and shape how they behave.

themes.title: Deconstruction
themes.text: Derrida read texts to expose ranked oppositions, such as voice over writing, and to unsettle them. He held that meaning is never fully present but arises from differences between signs.

themes.title: Difference that creates
themes.text: Deleuze treated difference as productive in itself, not merely as the opposite or negation of identity. He criticised thinking that reduces everything to sameness, opposition and resemblance.

reacted_against.text: It grew out of structuralism but turned against the idea of a self-present subject as the origin of meaning, as in Sartre's starting point, and against claims to firm foundations and stable meaning.

links.label: Habermas's critique of postmodernism
links.reason: Habermas argued that postmodernism contradicts itself and sought to rehabilitate modern reason against it.

links.label: the decentred subject
links.reason: Existentialism's critique of foundations and grand narratives, and Nietzsche and Heidegger in particular, shaped Derrida and Foucault.

links.label: Husserl deconstructed
links.reason: Derrida's Voice and Phenomenon criticises Husserl's founding 'principle of all principles'; Foucault rejected Sartre's privileging of the subject.

links.label: Butler's poststructuralist feminism
links.reason: Feminist critical theory has a poststructuralist strand (Judith Butler), and analytic feminists also draw on Foucault and Butler.

thinkers.name: Gilles Deleuze
thinkers.summary: Deleuze was one of the most influential and prolific French philosophers of the late 20th century. He saw philosophy as the creation of concepts and called himself a pure metaphysician. Besides studies of earlier philosophers and the arts, he wrote major books with Félix Guattari.

key_ideas.text: Difference is productive and comes first; it is not just the negation of identity.
Philosophy is the creation of concepts, alongside science and art as equal modes of thought.
With Guattari he described desire as a productive force running through society, rather than something rooted only in family figures.

Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Michel Foucault
thinkers.summary: Foucault was a French historian and philosopher linked with structuralism and post-structuralism, with wide influence across the humanities and social sciences. His histories of prisons and of sexuality traced how modern knowledge and power grew up together.

key_ideas.text: Genealogy traces how ideas and institutions arose from accidents and conflicts, not from pure origins.
Power and knowledge are bound together, as when an examination both reveals and controls the examined.
Modern discipline works through observation and 'normalisation', judging people against standards of normal behaviour.

Ask me one question at a time and finish with a five-question quiz.

thinkers.name: Jacques Derrida
thinkers.summary: Derrida, born in Algeria, founded deconstruction, a way of criticising literary and philosophical texts and also political institutions. His fame reached far beyond philosophy, into literary theory, architecture and politics.

key_ideas.text: Deconstruction reverses and unsettles ranked oppositions in philosophy, like essence over appearance.
Différance: meaning comes from a play of differences between signs and is never fully present.
Deconstruction aims at justice and at the least violence, even though full justice can never be reached.

name: Feminist Philosophy

tagline.text: Philosophy that challenges theories favouring men and rethinks sex and gender.

date_range: 1970s – present as an academic field (forerunners: Wollstonecraft, Beauvoir 1949)
description: Philosophy that criticises institutions and theories that have favoured men and rethinks sex, gender, knowledge and ethics.
debatable: Not a single school but a field that works within every tradition (analytic, continental, pragmatist; SEP §3).

questions.text: Why have so many institutions and ideas favoured men, and what would a just society look like?
Is being a woman something you are born as, or something you become?

questions.text: What changes when philosophy takes care, dependency and women's lives seriously?

themes.title: Ending gender-based oppression
themes.text: Feminism is both a way of thinking and a political movement aimed at ending oppression based on gender. Wollstonecraft's analysis of the condition of women in modern society still keeps much of its original radicalism. Beauvoir showed how a masculine way of thinking uses sexual difference to build a system that oppresses women.

themes.title: The 'neutral' view was male
themes.text: Philosophy often claimed to speak from a neutral, universal point of view. Feminists showed that these supposedly neutral approaches were in fact shaped around men. Beauvoir, asking what it had meant to her to be a woman, came to see that the world around her had always been a masculine one.

sources.section: 7. The Second Sex: Woman As Other

themes.title: Starting from embodied lives
themes.text: Feminist philosophers start by seeing people as embodied, and their work tends to be contextual and rooted in lived experience. Beauvoir's study of women's lived bodies is a founding example.

themes.title: Woman as the Other
themes.text: Beauvoir argued that men have been treated as the essential being and women as the Other. Myths of femininity trap women in that role, which is why she says one becomes a woman.

themes.title: Education, independence, equal rights
themes.text: Early feminists argued that women need education, reason and the means to support themselves. Wollstonecraft called for women's rights and representation; Taylor Mill's essay demanded equality in all rights.

reacted_against.text: It challenged institutions and theories that have historically favoured men, and philosophy's claim to speak from a neutral, universal point of view.

thinkers.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
thinkers.summary: Wollstonecraft was a moral and political philosopher whose analysis of women's condition in modern society still reads as radical. She is best known for A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), and she also wrote on education and politics and influenced travel writing and the Romantic movement.

key_ideas.text: Women should become rational, independent beings whose worth comes from self-command and knowledge, not appearance.
Education is key: girls should be trained in mind and body and taught skills to support themselves.
Women should have civil and political rights, and even their own elected representatives.

thinkers.name: Harriet Taylor Mill
thinkers.summary: Harriet Taylor Mill worked so closely with John Stuart Mill, whom she married in 1851, that their contributions are hard to separate. How much she wrote and how much she shaped his thinking is still contested, but today there seems to be general agreement, though some commentators dissent, that she was the main author of 'The Enfranchisement of Women' (1851).

key_ideas.text: Women deserve equality in all rights, political, civil and social, not just the vote.
A woman who earns part of the family income cannot be dominated the way a wholly dependent wife can.
J. S. Mill credited her with shaping key works, calling On Liberty their most directly joint production.

thinkers.name: Simone de Beauvoir
thinkers.summary: Beauvoir was a philosopher, novelist, feminist and activist, and a major figure in French existentialism after the war. She is best known for The Second Sex (1949). She was often regarded as merely the 'midwife' to Sartre's existential ethics rather than a thinker in her own right, yet decades of scholarship, mostly by feminist scholars, have secured her a place in philosophy.

key_ideas.text: Woman has been made the Other, while man is treated as the essential being.
